news.title: Ilhan Omar Says She Can't Stay at Home After Raid Amid Death Threats
news.text: Democratic U.S. Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota on Wednesday said that she cannot continue living in her Washington, D.C.-area home due to death threats and fears over her publicly available address, following the federal raid she accused the Trump administration of initiating to intimidate voters. “Obviously, I can't continue to live there,” the congresswoman told Chris Hayes on MS NOW Wednesday evening. "So have to figure out where to move to.” During the interview, Omar recounted waking up around 6 a.m. October 12 to Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents pounding on the front and back doors of her home while she, her husband and their 20-year-old son were inside. She described the raid as chaotic, saying her family scrambled to get dressed and downstairs as they tried to understand what was happening. “You don't show up to somebody's house that early in the morning unless you're trying to freak them out. And, you know, it obviously did freak all of us out,” she said. Omar said she had returned from traveling in the early morning hours and had been asleep for only a couple of hours when agents arrived. She initially thought something was on fire. She estimated that 15 to 25 agents searched the house room by room, over four to five hours. Authorities took 17 items, she said, including an older phone, her daughter's first phone, a recently replaced phone, keepsakes, a camera dating to the 1960s, a Somali phrase book and notebooks. “I was surprised when they handed me the receipt for the items they'd taken,” Omar said, noting the lengthy search. She said she was unable to call her attorney until about an hour into the operation and spent that time sitting on the couch and staring at the warrant, which she said covered electronics. Omar described the search as intrusive but said the agents behaved in a “decent” manner. She also said they did a “really good job” of putting everything back in its place, even folding some of her clothes. Newsweek reached out to the Department of Justice (DOJ) and Omar’s office for comment. Omar Is Asked If She's Related to Ex-Husband During the interview, Omar addressed long-running allegations that she married her brother, saying she was not aware of being related to her former husband. The congresswoman traced the rumor to a Somali blog post that she said right-wing conspiracy theorists in Minneapolis later picked up, pointing to “random people” who claimed she had introduced them to the man. "They just kind of went and found random people who were like, 'she introduced us. She introduced him to us and said he was her brother,' which is, you know, insane. I mean, I don't know those people that they talk about," Omar said. When Hayes asked whether she was related to the man, she replied, “Not to my knowledge.” The exchange has circulated on social media, where users have reacted to Omar's response and the renewed attention to the long-running allegation. Omar Says Trump Is Behind the Investigation Omar said she believes President Donald Trump has "everything to do with it," pointing to his longstanding attacks on her and his ongoing calls for her to be deported. “The people who knocked at my door searching for papers literally have his papers. They are the ones who processed those to come to the U.S.,” she said, referring to documents related to her late father. The DOJ previously told Newsweek that the October 12 search was part of “an ongoing federal criminal investigation” and said that HSI had executed a judicially authorized search warrant in Washington. The probe reportedly concerns fraud allegations involving Omar's immigration and naturalization paperwork. The congresswoman has not been charged in the investigation. Department of Homeland Secretary Markwayne Mullin described the investigation as a “strong case” in an October 16 interview on The Charlie Kirk Show, saying agents had executed multiple search warrants and investigators expected to present their case to a grand jury. He also suggested coordinated immigration fraud could be prosecuted under federal racketeering laws. After the raid, Washington, D.C., U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro confirmed a separate investigation into the congresswoman's financial disclosures, Newsweek previously reported. The investigation comes as Trump has renewed attacks on Omar's background and citizenship. At a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on October 12, Trump criticized Omar's Somali origins and questioned her right to invoke the U.S. Constitution. “She’s a disaster. She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military,” Trump said. On October 13, Trump also called Omar a “terrible person” and declined to take a position on whether he wanted her deported. Asked by Hayes whether she believes the investigation could lead to criminal charges or an attempt to revoke her citizenship, Omar said she takes the possibility “very seriously.” Omar also pushed back against Trump's characterization of her as wealthy, describing herself as working class and saying she lives a relatively modest life with her family. She argued that the investigation and timing of the search were intended to frighten her and discourage people from casting their ballots ahead of the November midterm elections. “Ultimately, their goal is to intimidate and scare people from wanting to participate and vote,” Omar said. “I think it's doing the opposite.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Steven Frank and Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: The Minnesota congresswoman described a chaotic early-morning search of her home and raised concerns about her family's safety.
news.author: Alex Backus

news.title: Trump Cheers On Violent Attacks on Protesters at Chaotic Rally
news.text:
President Donald Trump cheered on what appeared to be a violent physical altercation during a chaotic rally in South Carolina on Wednesday that saw multiple protesters disrupt the MAGA event.

Trump, 80, appeared at the rally to support Republican candidate Darline Graham ahead of the midterm elections, where she is in a fierce battle against Democrat Annie Andrews. The president backed Graham in the primary to replace her late brother, Lindsey.

However, it was a brutal fight in the audience at Clemson University that seized Trump’s attention, even causing him to pause his speech to comment on the brawl in graphic detail.

His rally speech had already been interrupted multiple times before the fight. At least three people were removed from the arena within Trump’s first 20 minutes on stage. The White House Press Pool reported that one yelled “traitor” and another “release the Epstein files” as she was led away by police.

The senior president repeated his regular claim that they were “paid protesters” earning $250 to disrupt his events, only to go home to be assaulted by their Trump-loving parents.

Then, talking about the “golden age of America” and discussing immigration and inflation, the president was distracted by what appeared to be a wild brawl on the auditorium floor.

While the start of the fight was not visible on cameras, conservative network Real America’s Voice aired a split-screen showing the aftermath, where security officers picked up a man in a blue T-shirt from the floor before escorting him out of the venue. Trump’s MAGA supporters cheered on, shouting “U.S.A!”

Footage captured by Fox News captured the scene in more detail, with punches appearing to be thrown.

The president seemed enthralled by the violent event, saying, “Wow, man, I loved that, I watched that. Man. You know, I watched that. I saw that. That was incredible. Wow. That was unbelievable.”

Finally checking, “Is everybody OK?,” Trump then swiftly said, while pointing to the scene of the melee, “Who is the guy who threw that punch?”

He repeated, “Who threw that punch?,” while his loyal supporters cheered wildly.

Trump continued to obsess over the incident. “I saw it, I’m looking right at that area, and this lunatic... he’s a very unattractive-looking guy.”

The president continued to discuss the brawl, again asking, “But who’s the guy that threw the punch?” He then appeared to identify the culprit, saying, “You are?” before adding that the person reminded him of MAGA-friendly boxer Evander Holyfield, who was also in attendance at the rally.

As he continued to narrate the fight, Trump said, “No, the guy stood up... and he got whacked. Man.”

Seemingly praising the protester, Trump added, “They don’t realize it’s really dangerous to do that. It takes... you gotta him credit. It takes courage to do that in a Trump rally.”

Once again delighting in reliving the violence, Trump said, “He got whacked... he started... with that screech, whatever the hell they do, whatever they practice. And as he’s in the process of the screech, he got whacked.”

MAGA influencer Eric Daugherty gleefully posted video of the aftermath, saying “MAGA MAN just THREW PUNCHES at a disruptive leftist who went berserk during the rally, and President Trump gave HIM a shoutout.”

He added, “This comes after ANOTHER leftist was slapped on the head while walking out.”

Daugherty also posted video showing a Trump supporter hitting a protester escorted out of the rally on Wednesday. A post including footage of the incident by NewsNation reporter Libbey Dean says the man was the sixth protester removed from the venue.

The White House Press Pool reported Trump was interrupted by hecklers six times in the initial nine minutes of his rally.

That included the president being repeatedly interrupted when attempting to finish a joke about how late Senator Lindsey Graham preferred his sister, Darline, to Trump.

“I hate to say this, Lindsay had a sense for people... He respected Darline more than any person alive,” Trump said, after his first interruption. “That includes me, Darline, and I wasn’t happy about it,” Trump noted, as his joke was paused again and the audience booed a protester.

“I don’t mind when they do that, but it’s always right at my punchline,” Trump complained. “I’ve had three punchlines... they time them beautifully, these people are serious losers.”

After another interruption, Trump made another attempt, stating, “Lindsey respected Darline more than any person on the planet and I’m not happy about it, I will never forgive him for that, because that included me.” The audience did not laugh at the joke.

The Daily Beast has contacted the White House and the South Carolina police for comment.
news.summary:

Trump, 80, appeared at the rally to support Republican candidate Darline Graham ahead of the midterm elections, where she is in a fierce battle against Democrat Annie Andrews. The president backed Graham in the primary to replace her late brother, Lindsey.

However, it was a brutal fight in the audience at Clemson University that seized Trump’s attention, even causing him to pause his speech to comment on the brawl in graphic detail.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

news.title: Why the stock market’s fragile calm faces a major test starting Friday
news.text:
US markets paused their slide this week as the tech sector found its footing following an AI sell-off sparked by high borrowing costs and doubts over data centre returns.

A bevy of upcoming catalysts will put this fragile pause to the test.

There could be a smooth transition where growing profits quietly push stock prices slowly higher over time, but there is also a real danger that the market suddenly snaps and suffers a major drop.

Last Friday, the S&P500 fell 1.1 per cent as a final wave of AI selling hit the tape. Such a move is not overly concerning, but what has traders worried was the intraday move in the Cboe Volatility Index, which went from under 16 to over 22 in two hours, a sign of significant investor fear and demand for options hedges.

Since 1990, only nine days have had a larger jump in the VIX on a smaller drop in the S&P500 than last Friday, according to SpotGamma.

Then there are the thin markets we have seen since the end of the quarter. On October 12, the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust saw its lowest full trading day volume since 2003. Reduced liquidity can be a harbinger of big gaps lower in prices.

The nervous, low-liquidity market is now preparing to run the most challenging gauntlet of risks we have observed all year, beginning this Friday.

Fiscal issues

This Friday, France faces a potential credit downgrade as Moody’s reviews its Aa3 long-term sovereign bond rating, which currently carries a negative outlook.

Add in continuing riots that threaten France’s retail and tourism industries and an upcoming presidential election in which far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has proposed cancelling part of the national debt and France’s fiscal situation looks untenable. Worse, the EU could face an existential crisis from the fallout.

An ECB bailout is likely inevitable, but unlikely to come before things get much worse. Watch for changes in “le spread”, the difference between German and French 10-year yields, currently 159 basis points.

On October 28, the UK Autumn Budget takes place. With UK borrowing costs at 30-year highs chancellor John Healey faces the challenge of matching public spending and tax revenue without smothering economic growth.

AI trade catalysts

As early as Friday, the official filing of Anthropic’s S-1 and the ensuing roadshow could provide a deeper look into the company’s financial performance and spending plans.

How much capital Anthropic plans to raise in its IPO will be the key for markets. Targeting a smaller raise could protect a higher valuation, but might trigger scepticism over how the AI firm will fund its massive infrastructure needs in a volatile bond market.

Conversely, a larger capital injection secures the necessary balance sheet for heavy cap-ex at the expense of a lower valuation.

The one-week period between October 28 and November 3 will see about half of the S&P500 index by market capitalisation report earnings, including tech heavyweights Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Apple and AMD.

Will capital expenditures continue to grow and is it doing so at the expense of free cash flow? Are there signs companies are monetising AI?

Military escalation into the midterms

As early as this weekend, Iran may launch a pre-emptive attack aimed at raising energy prices in a bid to influence US midterm elections.

It has already stepped up attacks on commercial shipping in recent weeks and escalation could see strikes on Persian Gulf shipping ports, refineries, pipelines or undersea internet cables.

The US has been bolstering its naval forces in the region despite Donald Trump’s pledge not to attack before the midterms on November 3.

Fed meeting

With influential FOMC members Fed vice-chairman Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams taking a wait-and-see approach, odds of a hike are low on October 28.

Markets could struggle to understand the need for a pause given September’s hotter-than-expected inflation report.

Back in July, it was suggested the Fed shouldn’t wait for September to raise rates, that upside inflation risks due to spiralling geopolitics were too great to ignore.

We are caught in a similar situation now.

Keep an eye on the number of dissenting votes, higher disagreement directly erodes the market’s confidence in the Fed’s decision.

A combination of any of these catalysts could be a most toxic brew for markets as financial risks act as multipliers rather than additions when sentiment turns.
news.summary: Markets paused their slide this week as the tech sector found its footing following an AI sell-off sparked by high borrowing costs and doubts over data centre returns.

news.title: Drones fall, strikes stall: How Musk's Starshield curbs hit Zelenskyy’s war effort
news.text: A disruption in the US military satellite internet service Starshield caused Ukrainian drones worth more than $1 million to fall from the sky and forced troops to halt almost all operations for three days, The New York Times reported, citing Ukrainian military commanders.A senior Ukrainian commander, identified only by his first name, Oleh, said dozens of armed drones were heading towards Russian military targets last week when their video feeds suddenly went fuzzy. The drones had lost their connection to ground-based pilots through Starshield, a Pentagon-funded satellite internet service, he said.Many of the drones crashed, costing his units more than $1 million worth of weaponry, according to the report.The development comes days after Donald Trump’s reported engagement with Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin over efforts to end the war in Ukraine. The MAGA supremo also recently eased sanctions on Russian oil.Oleh said the disruption forced his units to suspend almost all operations for the next three days, including strikes on Russian command posts and fuel hubs. Such attacks help protect Ukrainian troops on the front lines and slow Russian advances, he said.The reported disruptions have added to the growing tensions between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump. Ukrainian troops said connectivity had improved after a week, but problems persisted.The Trump administration has issued mixed statements on the issue, denying that any changes were made to satellite internet services in Ukraine while also saying that service had been restored.Ukrainian officials fear the disruptions were ordered to punish Kyiv for attacks on Russian oil refineries and pressure it into making concessions in the war. Ukraine has also reported gaps in US military intelligence sharing and delays in deliveries of American interceptor missiles. US officials have denied deliberately disrupting these services.What is Starshield and how does it affect Ukraine?Starshield is a military-grade satellite communications system developed by SpaceX, the company owned by Elon Musk. It is a more advanced sister system to Starlink, which is widely used by Ukrainian forces for communications and drone operations.European countries pay for Ukraine's access to Starshield. However, the advanced system is not available to all Ukrainian troops. Many units rely on it to operate drones while using standard Starlink connections for basic communications.Ukrainian officials have reported slowdowns affecting both Starshield and Starlink.Musk has said that Starshield is controlled by the Pentagon. However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio added to the confusion when he said on Wednesday that SpaceX determined access to both Starlink and Starshield.According to Ukrainian officials, the initial disruption caused drones to lose their connections at speeds as low as 40 miles per hour. Connectivity has since improved, but drones reportedly continue to lose their connections when travelling faster than 100 miles per hour.While some drone models can operate at these lower speeds, others need to fly faster to hit their targets, the report said.The restrictions have also affected interceptor drones used to bring down Russian drones targeting Ukrainian cities, Zelenskyy said.Ukraine is now looking for alternative ways to operate its drones, fearing that satellite connectivity could be restricted again or cut off entirely. Military commanders said the search for alternatives was diverting soldiers' attention from battlefield operations.US denies deliberately restricting satellite servicesUkrainian officials have sought clarification on who ordered the reported restrictions on Starshield and Starlink and why.A White House official told The New York Times that there had been no changes to satellite internet services in Ukraine.Trump also denied responsibility for any changes, saying on Friday that it “wasn’t me” and that “from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”Rubio said a day later that a Starlink slowdown in Ukraine had “sort of happened” but added that “my understanding is it’s been restored.”Zelenskyy has described the changes to Starshield as “a planned operation”.On NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said that “President Trump and Secretary Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge.”The issue has also drawn criticism from US lawmakers across party lines, with calls for the Trump administration to restore Ukraine's satellite connectivity.After a group of lawmakers spoke with Zelenskyy over a video call on Monday, Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina said the Ukrainian president had “confirmed ongoing Starlink disruptions, reported interruptions to critical US intelligence sharing and raised concerns about delays in air-defense interceptors.”Tillis also criticised Washington's approach towards Moscow, saying: “Degrading Ukraine’s satellite communications, weakening its air defenses and easing sanctions against Russia only embolden Putin and prolong this war.”He was referring to a move by Trump to allow the US to buy Russian diesel fuel.On Tuesday, Zelenskyy said he had a “substantive discussion” with Rubio about Starshield, shortages of missile interceptors and recent disruptions to early warning systems for Russian ballistic missile attacks.Rubio rejected claims that the US had withheld warnings about Russian attacks on Ukraine, calling them “simply not accurate”. He also said Patriot interceptors were in short supply worldwide.“Nothing is being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” Rubio said.Ukrainian troops struggle to adapt to restrictionsDespite the conflicting statements from Washington, Ukrainian commanders said the effects of the reported restrictions were evident on the battlefield.Brigadier General Andriy Biletsky, who recently took command of thousands of troops in the Center Grouping of Forces in eastern Ukraine, said Ukrainian forces were adapting to the new speed limits.Before the restrictions, Ukrainian drones using Starshield could fly at speeds of up to 250 miles per hour while maintaining a stable connection, Biletsky said.The formal speed limit had already been 100 miles per hour, but it had not been enforced, he added.This could allow the US to maintain that the system's rules had not changed, even as Ukrainian forces experienced a significant impact on the battlefield, the report said.Biletsky said that even if Ukraine managed to modify its attack drones to operate within the speed limits, interceptor drones used against Russian jet-powered weapons would remain at a disadvantage.These interceptors need to fly faster than incoming drones to bring them down. Russian jet-powered drones can travel far faster than 100 miles per hour.“Reducing the speed limits for air defense is a painful decision that literally undermines the protection of our cities, first and foremost,” Biletsky said. “So when the Pentagon took this step, it was undoubtedly an unfriendly move toward Ukraine’s civilian population.”Ukrainian commanders told The New York Times that they believed the restrictions were the result of a political decision rather than a technical problem. They said troops had long feared that Washington could use satellite connectivity as leverage to push Kyiv into making concessions.Oleh recalled receiving a series of angry calls from soldiers as his drones fell from the sky last week. Troops scrambled to redirect the drones and save as much equipment as possible.He said soldiers felt abandoned and argued that Ukraine should stop viewing the US as an ally.Lieutenant Yuriy Butusov, a company commander with Ukraine's 23rd Assault Regiment in the Khartia Corps, said the slower connections had severely affected his troops' operations.He said the disruption had effectively given Russian forces “a vacation day”.“This day without Starlink saved many lives and many trucks for Russia, unfortunately,” Butusov said.“It’s a big cost for us,” he added. “And much more blood. Our blood.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

news.title: Witkoff Reveals US Treasury Working With Putin’s Envoy on Economic Ties
news.text:
US President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff publicly confirmed Wednesday, Oct. 21, that Washington and Moscow are discussing future trade and economic cooperation alongside negotiations to end Russia’s war against Ukraine, revealing that the US Treasury Department is working directly with Kremlin economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev.

The disclosure came during Witkoff’s meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, where discussions extended well beyond peace proposals to include Russian diesel shipments to the US, financial arrangements and potential fertilizer exports.

“Our Treasury Department is working with you now independently,” Witkoff told Dmitriev during the meeting.

He said the contacts were helping both governments assess possibilities for renewed economic relations, which Washington was also discussing with Ukrainian officials.

The remarks provide explicit confirmation that the Trump administration has been pursuing economic engagement with Moscow, even as the US maintains extensive sanctions imposed over Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

They are particularly significant because Washington largely suspended official bilateral trade and investment engagement with Moscow following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, although limited commercial trade continued.

Witkoff reveals direct Treasury talks with Putin’s economic envoy

Dmitriev, the chief executive of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) and Putin’s special representative for international economic cooperation, has played a central role in Moscow’s contacts with the Trump administration.

Addressing Dmitriev directly, Witkoff praised his contribution to discussions between the two governments.

“You’ve been outstanding, Kirill,” he said.

Witkoff described the economic discussions as an indication of the opportunities that might become available if relations between Washington and Moscow improve.

He also revealed that the US was speaking openly with Ukraine about potential economic developments following the war.

“We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is ended,” Witkoff said.

His comments did not establish whether the Treasury Department’s contacts concerned sanctions relief, investment, banking arrangements or specific commercial agreements.

Nor did he identify the Treasury officials involved or explain what commitments, if any, Washington had made.

The contacts are notable because the US Treasury Department sanctioned Dmitriev and RDIF in February 2022, identifying the fund as part of the financial network supporting Putin’s government.

Treasury also administers and enforces major US financial sanctions on Russia through its Office of Foreign Assets Control.

Witkoff’s comments therefore raise questions about how discussions with Dmitriev fit into Washington’s broader sanctions policy and whether the administration is exploring ways to restore economic relations with Moscow.

US and Russia have had limited trade since 2022

The acknowledgment represents a departure from the sharply restricted economic relationship that followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In 2022, Washington imposed sweeping financial and trade restrictions on Moscow, including measures affecting Russian banks, energy imports, technology exports and investment.

The US also withdrew Russia’s normal trade relations status, exposing Russian imports to higher tariffs.

Formal bilateral engagement on trade and investment issues was largely halted, although commerce between the two countries did not end entirely.

According to the US Trade Representative, American goods trade with Russia totaled approximately $4.4 billion in 2025, compared with about $36 billion in 2021.

Against this backdrop, Witkoff’s confirmation that Treasury officials are working with Dmitriev indicates that the administration is considering future economic opportunities beyond the narrow trade that has continued under existing restrictions.

The remarks do not establish that Washington has lifted its broader Russia sanctions or agreed to restore normal trade relations.

Putin confirms Russian diesel shipments, offers fertilizers to US

The economic discussions were not limited to prospective cooperation after the war.

Witkoff thanked Putin for removing Russian diesel export restrictions, saying the decision would benefit American consumers and help ease pressure on global fuel markets.

He said Trump was deeply grateful, particularly because farmers and truck drivers had been affected by higher diesel costs.

Putin responded by claiming that global diesel prices had fallen between 5% and 6% following the announcement of Russian supplies to the US.

He said Moscow was preparing several tankers to begin deliveries, with the first carrying 40,000 metric tons of diesel and scheduled to depart within two or three days.

Additional shipments would follow, Putin said, adding that financial arrangements needed to be finalized to ensure the transactions could proceed.

The Russian leader also offered to supply large quantities of fertilizer to the American market, referring to Trump’s concerns about US farmers.

The discussion revealed that the two governments were addressing not only the political implications of closer economic cooperation but also practical questions about deliveries, payments and trade.

Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov later confirmed through Interfax that the diesel arrangement was discussed during the meeting and that practical implementation had begun following Washington’s decision to ease certain restrictions.

The diesel deal comes amid criticism in Washington that increased Russian energy exports could provide Moscow with additional revenue while its military continues attacking Ukraine.

Despite the emphasis on trade, Witkoff said ending Russia’s war against Ukraine remained a central objective of his visit.

He proposed resuming trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, suggesting that technical teams begin examining the next steps toward a settlement.
news.summary: Witkoff confirmed direct US Treasury talks with Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev on economic cooperation alongside Ukraine peace negotiations. Putin outlined Russian diesel shipments to the US and offered fertilizer exports.
news.author: Kyiv Post

news.title: US declares 'cyber warfare' on scam centres as seniors lose $7.7 bn
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 22 (IANS) The Trump administration is, for the first time, turning offensive cyber weapons on foreign scam centres, top officials have said, as Homeland Security disclosed that Americans over 60 lost $7.7 billion to cybercrime in 2025 and the Secret Service reported recovering thousands of child abuse videos. “With the executive order that you signed, for the first time ever, we are using offensive cyber capabilities to dismantle, disrupt, and disable these foreign scam centres. That has never been done before,” White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller told President Donald Trump at a White House roundtable on cybercrime and scams on Wednesday. “So you have effectively declared cyber warfare against the cyber criminals, and that is saving the pensions, the life savings, the retirement accounts, the earnings of countless American citizens,” Miller said. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said the department brought “CyberCom and NSA, and the exquisite capabilities” to the effort. “We’re feeding our deep intelligence and tracking data on overseas cyber networks directly to the National Coordination Center and Homeland Security Task Force,” he said. “We’ve also seen there’s a very clear connection between transnational cyber syndicates and enemy militaries and how they fund themselves,” Hegseth said, without naming any country. Trump said his August national security memorandum unleashed private sector “tools and resources” to “undertake offensive and defensive actions to stop the hackers”. Officials did not say which scam centres had been hit or where. Miller cast the campaign alongside Trump’s trade agenda, speaking of “entire foreign economies that are propped up on stealing from American seniors”. “America is not a pile of treasure for other countries and other people and other scammers all around the world to loot for themselves,” he said. Older Americans were described as the main targets. “When you get into what is going on, the elderly population, over 60, as just in 2025 through cybercrimes, lost 7.7 billion in their income,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said. “That’s retirements that are completely wiped away.” Miller described the “grandparent scam”. “Your grandmother, your grandfather, your parents, they get a phone call saying a loved one has been arrested, wired $10,000 right away to get them out of jail, except nobody was arrested, nobody’s in jail, and the money goes to a foreign scam centre,” he said. “We want to protect our seniors because the seniors almost more than anybody are really victims of what we’re talking about today,” Trump said. He advised victims to “seek out help from trusted family members”. Mullin also detailed action against online child exploitation. “Underneath Secret Service alone, they have recovered 14,600 child abuse videos, as the First Lady has so eloquently said, take it down, and over 35,600 images,” he said. He highlighted the Homeland Security Investigations campaign “Know to Protect”, which he said was “educating families on how to protect themselves from digital extortion”. “Behind every statistic is a human life,” Mullin said. Trump said the administration was “aggressively confronting the sexual extortion rackets that have wrecked the lives of too many young people, and in some cases even tragically led victims to take their own lives”. He credited First Lady Melania Trump, “who led a successful bipartisan effort to pass the Take It Down Act”. Attorney General Todd Blanche said: “We’re also meeting the serious threat of sextortion head-on.” “By taking on these cyber criminals on offence and defence, we watch out for our warriors, we watch out for American citizens, and we secure the homeland,” Hegseth said.

news.title: How Ukraine War Triggered Europe's Biggest Migration Wave Since World War II
news.text: Europe is witnessing waves of protests across several countries, including France, Spain, Portugal, Italy and Albania, with the high cost of living, housing shortages and economic pressures emerging as common themes. While US President Donald Trump has linked the unrest in France to migration and Islam, Europe has mostly been dealing with the aftermath of one of the continent's biggest refugee crises in modern history: the displacement caused by the Russia-Ukraine war. Largest displacement crisis in Europe since World War IIBy the end of 2025, there were 5.9 million Ukrainian refugees worldwide, with more than 5 million hosted across Europe, according to UNHCR."The war in Ukraine has been the fastest-growing and largest displacement crisis in Europe since World War II and has precipitated a regional refugee response of commensurate scale," UNHCR said. As the war entered its fourth year, Ukraine became the world's second-largest source country for refugees after Venezuela. Refugees and asylum seekers in EuropeIn 2025, Ukrainians were the largest refugee and asylum-seeker population in Europe, ahead of Syrians and Afghans. The arrival of millions of Ukrainians since 2022 has placed additional pressure on housing, education, healthcare and social services across several European countries."The refugee crisis in Ukraine represents an unprecedented burden for Europe," Habitat for Humanity said, noting that millions of displaced Ukrainians have faced challenges accessing housing, healthcare, education and social services.Moreover, several Central and Eastern European countries were not major destinations for asylum seekers before the war and were forced to rapidly expand their capacity to accommodate large numbers of refugees.Refugees from Ukraine into EuropeThe war triggered an unprecedented surge in Ukrainian migration to Europe. Before the invasion, the number of Ukrainian refugees and asylum seekers in European countries was relatively small, standing at around 30,000 in 2021. Following Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, the figure surged to more than 5.6 million."The historic mass outflow of people fleeing the unprovoked Russian war of aggression against Ukraine has placed significant pressures on the reception capacities of OECD and EU countries," the OECD said, adding that access to housing remains among the most pressing challenges facing refugees.Where did Ukrainians move within Europe?While Ukrainians spread across the continent, Germany, Poland, Czechia, the United Kingdom and Spain emerged as the largest destinations. Together, these five countries hosted about three million Ukrainian refugees, accounting for roughly 61 per cent of the total hosted in Europe. Romania, Moldova, Slovakia, the Netherlands and Ireland were among the other major destinations. The US military has quietly begun withdrawing troops from bases across the Middle East, while Washington is ordering diplomatic personnel to leave several missions in the region, NBC News has reported.

The moves come as President Donald Trump considers launching a new wave of attacks on Iran, and the withdrawals resemble preparations made by the Pentagon and State Department ahead of the initial US-Israeli strikes in February, NBC reported on Wednesday, citing two American officials and two people familiar with the matter.

American troops stationed in Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait are among those being relocated, according to the report. Washington reportedly intends to maintain a limited presence at its regional bases, including personnel responsible for air defenses and security.

Ahead of the February 28 attack, the Pentagon withdrew large numbers of troops from potentially vulnerable bases to shield them from expected Iranian retaliation. Tehran accused Washington of using Gulf residents as “human shields” after thousands of American service members took shelter in civilian hotels and office buildings.

US Central Command spokesman Timothy Hawkins declined to discuss the reported troop movements, saying American forces were regularly repositioned to “optimize mission readiness” and remained prepared to defend US personnel and interests.

The State Department has also ordered non-essential personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, citing escalating attacks by Yemen’s Houthi movement against civilian airports and other critical infrastructure.

Reuters reported that Washington was preparing additional diplomatic withdrawals across the Gulf, citing US officials, but State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott described reports of further withdrawals as “inaccurate.”

The developments come amid reports that senior US military officials have presented Trump with options for renewed strikes against Iran. According to NBC, the proposals include attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities, underground installations and strategic islands, including Kharg Island, a critical oil export hub, and Qeshm in the Strait of Hormuz.

Some of Trump’s advisers, including Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, have reportedly advocated resuming military operations to increase pressure on Tehran. Others have warned against launching another major campaign without a clearly defined objective.

Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, holding closed-door talks with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu just days before Israel’s October 27 parliamentary elections. Netanyahu is seeking another term amid mounting criticism of his handling of the wars in Gaza and Iran, while Trump has publicly endorsed his reelection bid.

Trump pledged earlier this month that the US would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections, while maintaining that military force remains an option if diplomatic efforts fail. Tehran has offered to restore normal navigation through the vital waterway within seven days if Washington lifts its naval blockade, eases oil sanctions and agrees to a broader cessation of hostilities.

news.text:
ANN ARBOR, United States: Rabbi Nadav Caine and his family gathered in their Michigan home to break challah bread for their weekly Shabbat meal, a brief respite from the acrimonious midterm election campaign dividing Jewish voters in their state.

The braided loaf, candles and sweet grape juice are weekly staples for many of Michigan’s roughly 100,000 Jewish voters who could help determine which party win a US Senate seat — and overall control of the chamber.

But while Caine is a longterm Democrat, he’s put off by the party’s candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

“I’m just mainly torn,” said Caine, 60.

El-Sayed, who won an upset Democratic primary victory on a populist message, is a Muslim — and like growing numbers of Americans strongly opposed to Israel’s government and US military aid. He’s also questioned Israel’s foundation as an explicitly Jewish state.

His outspoken defense of Palestinians and messaging missteps in the wake of a 2026 attack on a Michigan synagogue have dented his appeal in one of the country’s largest Jewish — and largely pro-Democrat — communities.

“The dilemma for us is that (El-Sayed) is someone that I strongly believe and sense doesn’t believe Israel has a right to exist as a state — or as a Jewish state — and is someone who fosters the sense that Jews deserve the antisemitism they receive,” said Caine, a rabbi at a conservative synagogue in Ann Arbor.

“I think for a public figure that puts Jews’ safety at great risk,” he added, describing himself as socially moderate and religiously conservative in his expansive home nestled among vibrant fall foliage.

‘Jewish safety’

Caine was among Jewish locals signing a petition of “Nonnegotiable” red lines, including Jewish sovereignty in Israel, in response to El-Sayed’s rise.

It demands candidates “treat Jewish safety, self-definition, statehood and political participation as baseline, nonnegotiable commitments.”

El-Sayed, seeking to become the first Muslim US senator, has not signed.

He drew criticism when he said “hurt people hurt people” after a Lebanese-born American drove an explosive-packed car into a West Bloomfield synagogue, before opening fire and killing himself.

El-Sayed says he has “been able to listen and learn ... and where my comments in the past have caused unnecessary pain, to apologize.”

Caine said that if El-Sayed wins on November 3, there’s still hope he could do more to embrace Jewish community “values.”

And El-Sayed, who has faced intense Islamophobia, including from his Republican opponent Mike Rogers and President Donald Trump, still enjoys some Jewish backing, particularly among leftists.

Businessman Kirk Dornbush, 65, staked out the October 8 televised debate between El-Sayed and Rogers in Grand Rapids, wearing a yarmulke and brandishing an “Abdul for US Senate” sign.

“Of the two candidates for Senate in Michigan only one of them has been discriminated against because of his religion,” he told AFP. “I’ve been discriminated against because of my religion and I’m Jewish so I’m voting with the guy who knows what it’s like.”

Bitter debate

Ahead of the bitter debate, during which Rogers accused El-Sayed of supporting jihadists, dozens of students marked the October 7, 2023, attacks on Israel at the University of Michigan’s Ann Arbor campus.

Attendees carried Israeli flags and heard an Israeli soldier whose speech was punctuated by shouts of “Free Palestine” from opponents.

“Many Jews here in Michigan are concerned about (El-Sayed’s) candidacy,” said University of Michigan graduate Michael Schostak, a Republican running for the institution’s governing board.

“I think the majority will not be voting for him ... That doesn’t mean they’re going to be voting for Mike Rogers.”

Both El-Sayed, 41, and Rogers, 63, recognize the importance of Jewish votes.

“What the polls aren’t picking up is our effort in the Democrat Jewish community,” said Rogers, who narrowly trails El-Sayed, at a factory outside Detroit.

“There’s about 100,000. Those numbers are swelling up. It’s huge for us,” added the Republican who calls his rival “anti-Jew.”

Rogers insisted Jewish voters, as well as Black, Indian American and Albanian American voters, would deliver him victory.

But University of Michigan-Dearborn politics professor Ronald Stockton estimated that one-third of Jewish were Republican, suggesting the remainder were “mostly not being won over by arguments that Jews are going to be at risk.”

During the October 7 vigil, an Ann Arbor Chabad House Rabbi Alter Goldstein said he hoped the winner would “have tolerance.”

“(But) hey, I’m not a prophet.”

news.title: Unacceptable, stupid: Macron hits back at Trump's remarks on France protests
news.text: Digital Desk | Paris, Oct 22 (IANS) French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders, including those "on the other side of the Atlantic", of attempting to exploit France's tense social climate for political gain following a weekend of violence and unrest. Protests in France over soaring living costs have attracted international attention. US President Donald Trump has blamed immigration for the unrest sweeping parts of Europe, warning that France and Italy risk further instability unless their governments tighten border controls, even as French authorities have attributed much of the recent violence to radical groups amid protests over education and rising living costs. Macron said there had been "foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath" of the looting reported in Paris and other French cities over the weekend. He criticised the comments made by several foreign leaders in response to the situation, describing them as both unacceptable and foolish. "And that has led to comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders," Macron said. When a reporter asked whether he was referring specifically to Trump, the French President replied, "Among others". Macron also rejected Trump's assertion that France was being overrun by migrants and Islamists, describing the claim as "completely false". He pointed to the circulation of AI-generated images portraying incidents that had never taken place in the country, arguing that such content was contributing to the spread of misleading narratives about the unrest. "AI-generated images depicting scenes that never actually happened in France. We've had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false," he said. Meanwhile, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said his office was prepared to provide the countries concerned with the necessary clarifications to prevent the further circulation of inaccurate information. He said the assistance would help them avoid spreading or amplifying false claims on social media. Macron also expressed frustration with those criticising France during the current situation, suggesting that their remarks reflected a lack of goodwill towards the country. "The fact is, all the people who are speaking ill of our country right now are people who don't love our country," Macron said. "So those people really bother me." "When I see leaders who are in the middle of election campaigns, whether in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic - who sometimes naively repeat AI-generated content or spread narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote about what happened in France - they're using our country for their own political campaigns... And we don't need that," Macron said.

The Tony Awards have nominated Ellis nine times for his direction of Broadway shows, usually musicals or big ensemble dramas like “Twelve Angry Men.” A 10th nomination for Ellis might be the charm, because “860,” despite being a one-man show, plays like a big opera without any singing. In the show’s opening moments, he sounded as if he were reading from a script. Was it Broadway debut jitters?

Whatever it was, Crystal’s script for “860” and Ellis’ fast-paced direction prevent a repeat of that brief soporific kerfuffle at the top of the show. Crystal leaps head first into that Palisades fire. Losing his home at 860 is the impetus for the comedian to remember how he and Janice came to that ranch-style house, built in the 1930s. They bought it with money earned from the TV comedy series “Soap” (1977-81), and it is here that “860” goes from a disaster drama to the full-blown comedy any Crystal fan would expect.

While “700 Sundays” is about Jack Crystal, “860” is all about his son Billy.

This one-man show goes back even earlier than “Soap” to Dec. 1, 1969, when the U.S. Defense Department held its Vietnam Draft Lottery – “they turned it into a television special!” — and Crystal secured himself a phenomenally high number, ensuring that he would not have to fight in the war. Voila, instead of a soldier, he became a stand-up comic!

Between the Palisades fire that brackets the show, “860” is a trip down memory lane, complete with lots of photos, films and videos. They show how Crystal’s hairline has vastly improved over the past 30 years ago. We also see his remarkable friendships with some of the biggest names in sports and show business. There’s Muhammad Ali, Robin Williams, Rob Reiner and Jack Nicholson, each the subject of an extended vignette where the comedy is delivered with healthy servings of schmaltz. Only Crystal’s memories of Mickey Mantle tip over into unrelieved sentimentality.

No one gets to be a superstar comic like Crystal without having a massive ego that needs constant nourishment. To commemorate the nine times Crystal hosted the Oscars, “860” features the April 1990 Life magazine cover that proclaims his “genius.” Donald Trump is brutally mocked when Crystal recalls his 2023 Kennedy Center Honor.

The show’s best political joke, however, comes when Crystal conjures up Williams to deliver a devastating Ronald Reagan-in-Hell howler that shocks while it brings down the house.
news.summary:
Despite the flames, this comic manages to deliver his greatest hits

news.title: ICE crackdown divides swing state candidates as GOP nominee vows to mandate sheriff cooperation
news.text: Republican Wisconsin gubernatorial nominee Tom Tiffany vowed Wednesday to mandate cooperation between local sheriffs and federal immigration authorities, drawing a sharp contrast with Democrat David Crowley over President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown during their general election debate. Tiffany said Wisconsin law enforcement agencies should be required to honor federal immigration detainers, arguing that coordination with ICE allows authorities to remove illegal immigrants accused of crimes while they are still being held in county jails. "I will make sure that local, county and state law enforcement coordinate with federal law enforcement," Tiffany said in the debate hosted by WISN-TV. VIRGINIA SANCTUARY COUNTY IGNORES 1,670 DETAINER REQUESTS OVER 2 YEARS, HOUSE JUDICIARY COMMITTEE FINDS Asked directly whether he would mandate that cooperation by law, Tiffany replied: "Yes, I believe we should. They should honor detainers." Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, said he would not support a blanket ban on cooperation with federal immigration authorities and agreed that immigrants convicted of crimes should be deported. But he called for restrictions on ICE operations, including barring contracts between local law enforcement and ICE, requiring judicial warrants for agents to enter jails and prisons and prohibiting agents from wearing masks. "We need to make sure that we're protecting people's civil liberties," Crowley said. Immigration enforcement has become an increasingly visible flashpoint in Wisconsin, where ICE arrests surged this summer as the Trump administration expanded its nationwide deportation push. TRUMP REAFFIRMS ICE ARREST POLICY AFTER CONFUSING GUIDANCE SPARKS ALARM AMONG AGENTS Trump's immigration crackdown has increasingly collided with state and local governments, putting sheriffs and police departments at the center of a national fight over how far local authorities should go to help federal agents carry out the president's mass deportation agenda. That debate is already playing out across Wisconsin. Twenty county law enforcement agencies in the state participate in ICE's 287(g) program, which allows designated local officers to perform certain immigration enforcement functions. Cooperation with ICE has also emerged as an issue in sheriff races in Sauk and Winnebago counties ahead of the November election. The latest available federal data showed ICE arrests in the state reaching new highs over the summer, with more than 2,100 people detained between January 2025 and the latest reporting period. news.text:
Is Belize Prepared to Welcome US Troop Under Shield of America?

Belize is open to strengthening its security partnership with the United States, but Prime Minister John Briceño says the country will not commit blindly. The proposed Shield of the Americas initiative comes as transnational criminals and drug cartels continue to threaten the region, making greater cooperation increasingly important. But after meeting briefly with U.S. Ambassador André Bauer today, Briceño made it clear that Belize must first understand what the initiative requires and whether it fits the country’s needs. Technical officials will now examine the proposal and determine what level of support Belize can realistically provide without compromising its national interests.

Prime Minister John Briceño

“Well we just had a brief discussion just now with the ambassador and the colonel. And what we’ve just talked briefly about it and I’m having the technical people to meet. news.title: Ilhan Omar believes Trump raid on home was meant to ‘intimidate and scare people’ from voting
news.text:
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., told MS NOW Wednesday night that she believes the raid on her home was to “intimidate and scare people” away from voting in the midterm elections.

Omar’s home in Washington, D.C., was raided by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) last Monday in connection to an investigation into potential immigration fraud. Authorities are probing whether Omar or her father lied on paperwork that helped her gain citizenship. Border czar Tom Homan has said that if the allegations are proven, Omar could be denaturalized.

Omar, who has largely avoided public scrutiny since the raid, gave her first interview on the subject on “All In with Chris Hayes” and suggested that the decision to investigate her was a last-ditch effort by President Donald Trump to appeal to right-wing influencers.

DEMOCRATS HAVE ‘DIRTY HANDS’ OVER COMPLAINTS ABOUT OMAR RAID WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION, EX-PROSECUTOR SAYS

Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home in Washington D.C. was raided last week in connection to an immigration fraud investigation. (Getty Images)

“I think they were like starting to lose faith that these were empty promises, and they had to do something, I believe, to say, ‘Hey, look, we raided her house. You know, now you can feel comfortable that we are doing something,'” Omar said. “I think … whether it’s Metro Surge, whether it is the voter rolls that they’re looking at, whether it’s the door knocks that you just spoke of, that is all to show these people that they’re doing something and to save face.” 

“Because they made this huge promise that there was somehow this massive … sort of undocumented people that were voting in American elections and that there is something that they need to go and fix.”

“And so they, you know, they’re going to try to gin up this sort of frenzy,” she added. “And, I think ultimately their goal is to intimidate and scare people from wanting to participate and vote.”

SOMALIS IN MINNESOTA UNLEASH FURY ON TRUMP AFTER FEDS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME

Rep. Ilhan Omar has largely avoided the public eye since the raid. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Despite that, Omar insisted that the raid had likely inspired people to vote in spite of the president.

“As I was driving up here today, we were getting calls that people, you know, are just like, there’s a massive line at early voting sites. And a lot of our staff that are, you know, helping people drive to go vote are saying, you know, ‘We don’t have the capacity to keep up with the requests that we’re getting of people who need assistance to get to the early voting site.’ I think it’s doing the opposite,” Omar said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment but did not immediately receive a response. 

ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND SNAPS OVER RUMORS SHE FLED US AFTER FEDERAL IMMIGRATION FRAUD RAID

President Donald Trump has suggested Rep. Ilhan Omar could go to jail if the allegations against her prove to be true. (Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images)

Prior to Tuesday night via a campaign video, Omar had not been seen publicly since before the raid on her home, which was first reported by Fox News Digital last week. Her husband, Tim Mynett, has been seen outside the residence walking their dog. 

Additionally, Fox News Digital has spotted a campaign aide bringing in food and both of her daughters arriving at the home two days apart.

Trump warned Tuesday from the Oval Office that Omar could be jailed if the allegations against her are true.

“Well, she could be. She could also go to jail,” Trump said. “You know, they keep talking about deportation. No, she could go to jail.”

“This is just my opinion,” he continued, before calling the congresswoman “a very dishonest person” who “hates our country.”

Fox News’ Peter D’Abrosca contributed to this report.

"WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of 'humanitarian'," he said in a post on X.Trump brushed off the comments by Witkoff -- a business friend whom he appointed roving envoy for the Ukraine, Iran and Gaza conflicts after he took office last year."Well, I guess you could say (it) for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out," Trump said when asked about his envoy's remarks."But you know, I wouldn't say anything one way or the other."US Vice President JD Vance defended Witkoff's comments."I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage," Vance said at an event in Ohio."Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done."(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: Trump Highlights Federal Crackdown on Cybercrime at White House Roundtable
news.text:
WASHINGTON—President Donald Trump said that nearly three-quarters of American adults have faced online scams or cyberattacks, as he convened top officials to review his administration’s efforts to stem more than $20 billion in reported losses.

“And this is just what’s reported,” Trump told reporters during a White House roundtable on Oct. 21.

War Secretary Pete Hegseth, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and FBI Director Kash Patel also attended the roundtable held in the East Room.

In March, the president signed an executive order directing federal agencies to coordinate against online fraud and cybercrime. The order also established a program to help victims recover their forfeited funds.

In August, Trump signed a National Security Presidential Memorandum authorizing vetted companies to conduct cyber surveillance and offensive cyber operations against transnational criminal organizations.

Trump said that federal law enforcement has since warned more than 10,000 Americans targeted by scammers, and stopped at least $1.6 billion in losses so far this year. They’ve also frozen close to $1 billion in cryptocurrency linked to overseas scammers, he said.

Speaking at the event, Blanche said social media companies Meta and X have been cooperating with law enforcement in identifying scam attempts.

“In April, the FBI and the Dubai Police announced the arrests of at least 276 individuals and the dismantlement of at least nine scam centers that targeted Americans,” Blanche said.

Mullin said that people over 60 lost $7.7 billion to cybercrimes in 2025.

“There’s a very clear connection between transnational cyber syndicates and enemy militaries,” Hegseth said. “If they can’t match us or beat us on the battlefield, which they can’t, then of course they try to move to the realm of cyberspace to attack.”

Speaking at the event, Patel highlighted the FBI’s Operation Blackout in Southeast Asia and Africa. He said the agency has demolished more than 20 compounds overseas and helped seize over $17 billion from these scam centers. Patel also highlighted how American tech giants like Meta, Google, Microsoft, and IBM have joined forces to combat cybercrime.

Americans lost an estimated $148.2 billion to online scams and crimes in 2025, about 26 percent more than the prior year, according to a report from the Consumer Federation of America.

More than half of all reported losses involve cryptocurrency, the report said.

A recent Consumer Reports survey also found that nearly 9 in 10 Americans have faced a cyberattack attempt or digital scam, and 17 percent have fallen victim.

“I would say it’s a very negative thing, but what we’re doing is very positive,” Trump said before wrapping up his speech at the roundtable.

“We'll put a dent—a very big dent—hopefully, in what’s been taking place for really many decades. And it’s gone totally unchecked.”
news.summary: The administration is putting 'a very big dent' in what has been happening for decades, the president said.

news.text: The trade agreement between India and the United States, which has been under negotiation for more than a year and a half now, is "pretty close" to conclusion, said US President Donald Trump, who indicated the final arrangement between the two nations would differ significantly from any earlier trade agreements signed by Washington.While speaking to reporters at the Oval Office, Trump was asked whether Washington and New Delhi were approaching an agreement.What Trump Said"They want to make a deal. We're going to make a deal. Pretty close, yeah," Trump said."It's going to be a much different kind of deal than we've made," he added.Trump did not elaborate on what would make the proposed agreement different from previous arrangements. He also did not specify a date for concluding negotiations or identify the remaining issues preventing a final agreement.His comments nevertheless suggested that Washington expected progress in talks that have been closely watched by businesses, exporters and investors in both countries.Timing Of The RemarkThe Republican leader's remarks came as Secretary of State Marco Rubio was visiting India and holding discussions with Foreign Minister S Jaishankar on further strengthening bilateral relations, focusing on sectors such as trade, energy, technology, defence and people-to-people ties. The timing places the president's comments against the backdrop of high-level diplomatic engagement between the two countries.Talking to The Indian Express earlier this week, Rubio assured that the India-US trade deal, which has been under negotiation for more than a year and a half now, was "weeks, not months" away. Earlier this month, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal met US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Milwaukee and Washington to discuss the finer aspects of the trade deal.India-US Trade DealIndia and the United States have been negotiating a bilateral trade arrangement aimed at expanding market access and addressing longstanding differences over tariffs, agricultural products, industrial goods and regulatory barriers.Trade negotiations have acquired additional significance under Trump's second administration, which has made tariffs and reciprocal market access central elements of American economic policy. The administration has argued that trading partners must offer American businesses greater access to their markets while reducing barriers affecting US exports.For India, the negotiations carry implications for major export sectors, including pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, textiles, electronics and information technology-related services. news.title: White House Strips Access to Reporter It Called a Sick Slur
news.text:
The White House has restricted access for the journalist whom it called a vile slur for people with Down Syndrome.

The Independent’s Andrew Feinberg was scheduled to serve as President Donald Trump’s print pooler on his Thursday trip to Sioux City, Iowa, but the White House suddenly revoked his assignment Wednesday without explanation, reports Semafor’s Maxwell Tani.

Feinberg is the same reporter who, on Tuesday, was viciously attacked by the president for asking about his proposed D.C. golf course, which the White House later tacked on with a vulgar insult.

Fox News reporters Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, condemned the decision in a statement Wednesday night.

“The White House Correspondents’ Association strongly objects to the decision to restrict a journalist’s coverage simply because the president didn’t care for their questioning. That is retaliation,” Heinrich wrote. “The American public’s right to an independent press depends on reporters being able to do their jobs without fear that challenging the president will cut off their access.”

The Daily Beast has reached out to the White House and Feinberg for comment.

Trump, 80, snapped at Feinberg in the Oval Office when asked about his plans for a golf course at East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C.

“Wait a minute. Wait, wait. Quiet. Quiet!” the president snarled, interrupting Feinberg’s question. “What’s wrong with you? Are you a sick person?”

“Not that I know of, sir,” Feinberg replied, to which Trump snapped back, “No, I actually think there’s something wrong with you.”

The White House’s anonymously run “Rapid Response” account gloated over Trump’s vicious attack with an even more obscene insult.

“@POTUS absolutely roasts Mongoloid Moron @AndrewFeinberg for his disgraceful behavior: ‘What’s wrong with you? Are you a sick person? I actually think there’s something wrong with you,’” the account wrote.

The insult against Feinberg used a slur that referred to a discredited Victorian belief that people with Down Syndrome had similarities to East Asian people, who were seen as racially inferior to whites.

Its stark offensiveness caused the World Health Organization to delete the term in the 1960s.

Vice President JD Vance tagged in shortly after, calling Feinberg an “imbecile.”

“President Donald J. Trump eviscerates imbecile ‘journalist’ Andrew Feinberg for misbehaving in the Oval Office,” Vance, a devout Catholic convert, wrote on his official account.

Feinberg replied to Vance, “Mr. Vice President, if you’re going to insult me, at least have the guts to tag my account.”

The Trump administration has repeatedly attacked reporters this term. Trump himself frequently singles out journalists, often female reporters, to belittle them in front of their colleagues, such as when he told Bloomberg News’ Catherine Lucey, “Quiet, piggy,” last November.

news.title: Meta ordered to pay New Mexico $25 billion for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook
news.text: A judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.Facebook’s deception was intentional and executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked, state District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew wrote in his ruling.“Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false,” he said.Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws for making misleading public statements about how it handled users' personal data. The case was brought after political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica harvested Facebook data to generate targeted political ads during the 2016 election season.The award will serve as a warning to tech companies that New Mexico will hold them accountable, state Attorney General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference.“This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” he said.Meta said the ruling and Torrez's office's approach to enforcement “makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico.”“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal,” C.J. Mahoney, the company’s chief legal officer, said in a statement.The Menlo Park, California, company has a market value of $1.8 trillion and brought in more than $200 billion in revenue last year. Company shares traded 2% higher after Wednesday's announcement, and it was scheduled to report its quarterly earnings later in the day.New Mexico goes it aloneIn August, Meta reached a settlement with nearly all states and territories — except New Mexico and Florida — to pay $18 billion and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms.The settlement ended a trial over teen social media addiction and resolved a pivotal case years in the making that sought to hold the tech giant accountable for the role its platforms played in undermining children’s mental health. The effort targeted features designed to grab young people’s attention.New Mexico didn’t join the multistate settlement, choosing to go after the company on its own.The director of a nonprofit that supports stronger policies toward corporations said $25 billion is “a drop in the bucket for Meta,” but demonstrates people want accountability.“Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information,” added Nidhi Hegde, executive director of the American Economic Liberties Project. 'Which is why we need more enforcers with courage and laws with actual teeth to rein them in.”At the trial, attorneys for the state cited a 2010 Washington Post op-ed in which Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote that the company didn't sell user data.“You have control over how your information is shared,” Zuckerberg said. “We do not and never will sell any of your information to anyone.”New Mexico officials sought fines of $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing the company would only change if its stock price were impacted.Meta's lawyers, meanwhile, asserted that the state failed to prove the company made misleading statements and that content moderation actually harmed people in New Mexico. They wanted the company to pay $3.4 billion at most and said an award many times larger would be unconstitutional.Although interest would accrue on the penalty during the appeal process, Meta could succeed in reducing the number of violations for which it is found liable.The $25 billion award far exceeds a $5 billion fine the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019.Peter Ormerod, an associate law professor at Villanova University, was surprised by the size of the New Mexico judgment because previous legal settlements over Cambridge Analytica were much lower.“It comes out to about $12,000 per person in New Mexico,” he said. “It’s quite unlike anything else we’ve seen.”Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violating consumer protection laws go toward education spending. It could take years for the state to get the money while the company appeals.Company argues that the state failed to prove harmThe trial focused on accusations Facebook deceived users about a breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to Cambridge Analytica. The now-defunct firm’s clients included Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign.Attorneys for New Mexico argued that the state's entire population was deceived, and that Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate.Meta’s lawyers argued the state failed to prove people were harmed by deceptive statements. Zuckerberg in a video deposition denied that Facebook profited off harmful content and said the company had to balance free speech with content moderation.In a partial win for the company, jurors rejected assertions that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.Meta lawyers said it has changed policies since the lawsuit was filed in 2021 and catches and removes an estimated 99% of content violating its standards.

news.title: Florida attorney accused of threatening to shoot ICE agents while trying to buy gun
news.text: A Florida attorney was arrested after she threatened to shoot ICE agents in the head while trying to buy a gun, federal authorities said. Homeland Security Investigations identified White as a Florida attorney in a post announcing her arrest on X. Authorities said White asked whether specific firearms could penetrate ballistic vests, then allegedly said she would target agentsâ heads if she could not breach their armor. FBI ARRESTS PROTESTER WHO THREATENED TO KILL ICE OFFICER'S FAMILY AT NJ DETENTION CENTER PROTEST, BLANCHE SAYS HSI Gulfport special agents responded, interviewed witnesses and located and arrested White, according to the release. The investigation began Sept. 23 after an agent with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives alerted HSI to the encounter at High Caliber Guns, according to a criminal complaint obtained by the Sun Herald. White entered the store around 11:30 a.m. and told employees, "I need a gun," according to the complaint cited by the outlet. She allegedly identified herself as an activist and protester and said she wanted a firearm for protection at a protest because she believed "ICE agents are becoming crazy and wild." But White also told an employee she wanted to buy a gun to kill ICE agents, according to the complaint. While discussing the weapons, White allegedly gestured toward her torso and asked whether the guns could penetrate an agentâs body armor. If they could not, she said she would need to "hit them in the head, shoulder, arm or leg," the complaint states, according to the Sun Herald. news.title: Trump’s Border Goons Spotted at Blue City’s Polling Site
news.text:
An elections supervisor in a heavily Democratic city says two Border Patrol trucks were parked at the city’s busiest early voting site on Monday.

Mark Earley, Supervisor of Elections in Florida’s Leon County, says he has filed a complaint with the FBI about the brief presence of federal agents at Northeast Branch Library in Tallahassee, the state capital.

“On Monday, October 19th at around 10:15 a.m., two Customs and Border Patrol vehicles parked at the Northeast Branch Library, our busiest early Voting site. This was shortly after the start of Early Voting here in Leon County,” Earley said. “The two vehicles appeared to stay for approximately 10 minutes before leaving the vicinity of the site.”

Earley said he has raised his concerns with local, state, and federal partners, whom he credited with being responsive. 

“I have lodged a formal complaint with the FBI, and to their credit, they are taking this seriously,” he added. 

Earley said intimidation and implied threats during the voting process are unacceptable.

“Voters should never experience intimidation from anyone when they are voting, and that includes being intimidated by law enforcement or any other governmental officials,” he said. “This nation belongs to the people. Government works for them. I will do everything in my power to ensure that our voters can vote in a fair election free from intimidation or implied threats.”

The Daily Beast has contacted the Department of Homeland Security, Border Patrol, ICE, and the FBI for comment.

Leon County is solidly Democratic. In the 2024 presidential election, Kamala Harris won by 11 points. As of Oct. 5, registered Democrats outnumbered registered Republicans by more than 30,000.

The sighting of federal agents at the Tallahassee voting site comes as DHS agents have been going door to door in several states, asking residents not only about their immigration status, but also whether they have registered to vote or voted in the past.

CBS News reported Wednesday that DHS agents are making these inquiries less than two weeks before Election Day. President Donald Trump claimed this summer that there were 250,000 people illegally registered—a number experts say is the result of false positives. Since Trump took office, CBS notes that only 156 people have been charged with voting fraud-related crimes.

Regional DHS accounts on X have been touting their efforts in places like northern California and in Kansas City.

In June, DHS launched a “surge” to seek out “criminal voter fraud” through Homeland Security Investigations, an arm of ICE, CNN reported. Internal department guidance said then that offices in nine states—Washington, Wisconsin, Missouri, Georgia, California, Pennsylvania, Nevada, New York and Connecticut—would launch investigations from early September to mid-October. “Overt” investigations so close to the midterms have typically been avoided because of a Justice Department policy against influencing elections.

But DHS is not required to follow the policy.

“While ICE Homeland Security Investigations is not able to comment on any active investigations, HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found,” a Homeland Security spokesperson told CNN then. “Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders.”
