news.title: FBI chief Kash Patel says $17 bn seized as US widens war on foreign scam centres
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 22 (IANS) FBI Director Kash Patel said the bureau and its partners have seized more than $17 billion from overseas scam compounds under Operation Blackout, as the Trump administration launched a government-wide crackdown on call centres and online networks that defraud Americans. "The Federal Bureau of Investigation, along with our partners at DOJ and the United States Attorney's offices, have seized over $17 billion from these scam compound fraud centres," Patel told a White House roundtable on cybercrime and scams chaired by President Donald Trump on Wednesday. "Seized it. That means that's money we got back." Patel, the first Indian-American to head the FBI, said the operation had "destroyed and demolished over 20 compounds" run by criminal syndicates. "Scam centres for the American public and the world are literally towns and ecosystems with traffic victims with cities and housing that they built an empire for criminal syndicates to fleece American citizens," he said. "They're in Southeast Asia. They're in Africa. They're in the Middle East." "They moved to Africa. We got them there, too," Patel said. "Just two weeks ago, we were in Ghana, Nigeria, and we arrested another 300 individuals and seized another $15 million being fleeced from American senior citizens through these scam centre operations." Attorney General Todd Blanche said that in April, "FBI and the Dubai Police announced the arrests of at least 276 individuals and the dismantlement of at least nine scam centres that targeted Americans", while prosecutors "unsealed charges against their managers and their recruiters". Trump, opening the session, said, "Federal law enforcement has been able to warn over 10,000 Americans targeted for victimisation, and we prevented $1.6 billion in losses, at least this year." "Federal law enforcement has also frozen nearly $1 billion of cyber currency, and tied to foreign scammers, shut down more than 500 fraudulent websites, and coordinated with technology companies to disrupt millions and millions of online accounts used by foreign criminals," he said. He added that authorities had "engaged with international partners to arrest hundreds of foreign scammers of all types, including scam call centres". Blanche said the State Department was now refusing entry to scam operators. "There is no corner of government from which these predators can hide," he said. "HSI and FBI are identifying them. The State Department is denying them visas, and our prosecutors are charging them." He did not say how many visas had been refused or which nationalities were affected. He said the Justice Department had set up a "new scam centre cell" with the Homeland Security Task Force so that "every case is built to take down not just one scammer, but the whole network". Its cyber-enabled scam initiative, he said, "deploys dozens of prosecutors across all 94 US attorneys' offices". He also said the department last month "seized Shinbee Criminal Marketplace and restrained $52 million on the same day that Treasury sanctioned it". Patel said technology firms including "Meta, Google, Microsoft, IBM" had "shut down internet trafficking and domain networks", and urged victims to report to the FBI. "No piece of information is too small," he said. "We are not waiting for the scammers to hit our citizens. We are going out there in full force," Patel said.

news.title: What happened during Witkoff and Kushner’s latest meeting with Putin  - St. Vincent Tribune – Daily St
news.text:
United States special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have wrapped up their latest meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin with the release of a retired American teacher from Russian custody.

On Wednesday, Witkoff visited with Putin at the Constantine Palace in Saint Petersburg, while Kushner attended virtually.

The two special envoys have taken a leading role in conflict negotiations under US President Donald Trump. Their last meeting with Putin came during a trip to Moscow in September.

The latest talks come as the Trump administration intensifies its efforts to secure a peace deal to end Russia’s nearly five-year-long war against Ukraine. The war began when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of the Eastern European country in February 2022.

But there are growing concerns in Kyiv that the Trump administration is backing away from its support of Ukraine.

Trump has fostered warm relations with Putin, and critics fear that he may be willing to yield to Russian demands to reach an agreement that would end Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War II.

Here’s what took place during the meeting:

Putin agrees to resume peace talks with Ukraine and US

The Russian president agreed on Wednesday to resume US-mediated peace negotiations with Ukraine for the first time in months.

A US official told Al Jazeera that Witkoff and Kushner proposed a “trilateral meeting at the technical level” that would focus on guaranteeing the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war had ended. The Ukrainians accepted the meeting when they met with the Americans on Tuesday in Oslo, Norway.

The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February, just days before the US and Israel launched their war against Iran.

The Kremlin, according to the Reuters news agency, said the new talks with Ukraine and the US may take place in Abu Dhabi and could start as soon as next month.

Russia frees retired US teacher

Wednesday’s meeting began with a goodwill gesture from Russia: the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher who has been held in Russia for more than four years.

Hubbard, 74, was arrested in 2022 and sentenced to more than six years in a Russian prison after he was accused of being a Ukrainian mercenary. The US has argued the former teacher was wrongfully detained.

Trump, who made a direct appeal to Putin for Hubbard’s release, posted on social media Wednesday that Russia did not ask for a prisoner swap “out of respect for” him.

A US official said Trump spoke with Hubbard by phone and reiterated his “unwavering commitment” to bringing home all Americans who are wrongfully detained abroad.

Hubbard is headed back to the US where he will be reunited with his family.

Putin called a ‘humanitarian’

Witkoff has faced growing criticism after calling Putin a “humanitarian” for his decision to release Hubbard.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” Witkoff said to Putin during Wednesday’s meeting. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you.”

That praise for the Russian president sparked bipartisan backlash from US lawmakers and human rights activists, who pointed to accusations of severe human rights abuses under Putin’s leadership.

“WTF, Steve?” US Senator Thom Tillis replied in astonishment on social media. Tillis, a member of Trump’s Republican Party, continued by writing that Witkoff should look up the definition of “humanitarian”.

“What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say,” he said. “You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a ‘humanitarian’.”

Tillis’s Senate colleague, Republican John Cornyn, echoed those thoughts.

“Putin is stone cold killer,” he wrote in response to Witkoff’s remarks.

US Senator Mark Kelly, who serves on the US Senate Intelligence and Armed Services Committees, also blasted Witkoff, calling Putin a “war criminal”.

“In what world is Putin a ‘humanitarian?’ He’s assassinated political rivals and journalists, bombed hospitals, and started a war that has intentionally killed tens of thousands of innocent people, including women and children,” Kelly, a Democrat from Arizona, said.

But members of the Trump administration defended Witkoff amid the outrage. During a visit to his home state of Ohio, Vice President JD Vance argued that Witkoff had “a job to get done”. He indicated that complimenting Putin likely aided the negotiations.

“I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage,” Vance told reporters.

At a White House event on Wednesday, Trump said Witkoff’s characterisation of Putin was a “good saying” for “that particular purpose”: to release Hubbard.

“But I wouldn’t say anything one way or the other,” the US president said.

Trump, Putin and Xi meeting gains steam

The Kremlin said a possible meeting between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping was discussed during Wednesday’s negotiations.

Russian officials said that, if the meeting is confirmed, it could take place next month on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.

“Given that all three heads of state may potentially take part in the summit in China, the subject of such a hypothetical meeting was indeed raised,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday.

“No specific proposals or agreements were discussed or put forward by anyone, either regarding the meeting itself or the possible agenda and content of that meeting.”

The three leaders have never before met for a dedicated trilateral visit.

news.title: US accuses Canada of election interference ahead of midterms  - St. Vincent Tribune – Daily St Vincent And
news.text:
The United States has accused Canadian politicians of trying to influence its midterm elections, pointing to Canada’s efforts to push back against President Donald Trump’s tariff campaign.

In a fact sheet released on Wednesday, the US embassy accused Canada of being dismissive of its allegations of election interference.

“The Canadian government brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances,” the fact sheet reads.

The two countries have been locked in a trade war since the start of Trump’s second term in 2025, with Canada responding to US tariffs with import taxes of its own.

But the US embassy identified public statements about the tariffs as being attempts to sway the November 3 midterm election.

Among the politicians singled out in the fact sheet was Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly. The fact sheet pointed to comments Joly made in August about responding to Trump’s tariffs.

“We’re also targeting products that will target states in the US. And so we’re being wise and strategic to put political pressure,” Joly said at the time.

The embassy also took issue with Joly’s meetings with Democratic officials in Boston and Chicago in September. When asked by a reporter what she thought might happen with regard to tariffs if Democrats won the midterms, she said, “That’s exactly why I’m meeting so many governors and potential presidential candidates.”

Joly has rejected the suggestion that her actions could amount to interference, saying Canada would never meddle in US elections. She said her meetings with US politicians, both Democratic and Republican, were about building Canada’s economy.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the US is to attract investments,” she told reporters on October 14.

The embassy also pointed to Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s calls for retaliatory measures on US products, as well as his government’s advertising campaign against Trump’s tariffs, launched last year.

The campaign, which featured clips of former US President Ronald Reagan criticising tariffs in a 1987 radio address, prompted Trump to call off trade talks with Canada in October 2025.

While the embassy laid out several examples of Canadian officials trying to influence US trade policy, it didn’t explain how those efforts amounted to interference.

Other instances of alleged election interference included Liberal MP Anthony Housefather saying he had campaigned in Florida on behalf of Democratic Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz, ahead of her primary election in August.

The fact sheet also accused individual Canadians of illegally participating in US elections, naming 11 people who had been charged or sentenced for voting between 2012 and 2024.

The sheet did not, however, present any evidence linking those citizens to a Canadian government effort to involve itself in US elections.

“All Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence U.S. elections in any way,” the US embassy’s statement said. “Americans decide America’s elections.”

The fact sheet comes a week after US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said Washington was closely watching Canada for signs of interference ahead of the midterms.

“We’re monitoring it, we’re evaluating it and if some of it becomes election interference then America will respond to it,” Hoekstra said in a podcast interview on The Really Big Show, according to The Canadian Press.

The US and Canada have long been allies, but relations have frayed since Trump returned to office.

Not only has the Republican leader triggered a trade war with Canada, but he has also repeatedly threatened to make Canada a 51st state.

There have also been reports that separatist leaders from Alberta had sought support from Trump administration officials ahead of a failed referendum on the province’s independence this week.

Ahead of Monday’s provincial vote, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed concerns about potential US interference in the referendum, saying Canada expected foreign governments to stay out of its elections.

“Our expectation is, to be absolutely clear, on foreign governments, United States included, is we don’t get ourselves involved in their elections, they don’t get themselves involved in our elections,” he told Global News.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the Prime Minister’s Office and Global Affairs Canada for comment, as well as the office of Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Industry Minister Joly.

news.title: Peter Thiel breaks with Trump over Iran war: 'We should not have done it'
news.text: Billionaire technology investor Peter Thiel said he's skeptical of the US war with Iran and does not believe the United States should have launched it, putting the major Republican donor at odds with President Donald Trump over one of the administration's defining foreign policy decisions, POLITICO reported. Thiel's remarks, delivered on October 12 at a private event, are his most explicit statements to be revealed publicly about the war with Iran and come less than two weeks before the midterm elections in which Trump's party is grasping to maintain power in Congress. The audio of Thiel's comments was obtained by Decoded by POLITICO from a lecture earlier this month. "I'm skeptical of [the war], I think we should not have done it," Thiel said. "There were a lot of mistakes that were made." Thiel added, "Maybe we don't have the hard power. Maybe we're going to lose the soft power war." In the full lecture, Thiel made clear his strong opposition to neoconservatives and Middle East wars. Despite his criticism of the Iran war, Thiel highlighted his continued support of Trump and suggested he wanted to protect the president. Still, Thiel's break over the war represents one of the most important examples to date of a fierce Trump ally sharing deep concerns about the conflict. The comments were part of Thiel's lecture series in Nashville, which Decoded has documented since their start this fall. In the latest lecture, Thiel issued extensive warnings about what he described as the unchecked power of the International Criminal Court, drawing on comments from Bush-era figures Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney. "I read the Cheney family's Trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [International Criminal Court] and avoid prosecution. Probably too late," Thiel said. "And I have come to suspect that the threat of an ICC arrest warrant is the sword of Damocles hanging over the Trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in Iran." Thiel also discusses meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in early 2024, after the October 7 attack, where he said he asked the president about his plans in Gaza. Thiel said Netanyahu told him, "I can't just Dresdenize it," referring to the Allied bombing of the German city of Dresden during World War II that killed roughly 25,000 people. The first big tech investor to back Trump in 2016, and then have a high-profile speaking role at the Republican National Convention that year, Thiel was also the biggest financial backer of super PACs supporting Vice President JD Vance's Senate campaign in 2022. POLITICO reported in March that Vance was "skeptical" of the U.S. striking Iran in the lead-up to the beginning of the war. news.title: Video game developer BioWare shuts down, next 'Mass Effect' canceled amid broader layoffs at EA
news.text:
Video game publisher Electronic Arts is shutting down the popular and influential game development studio BioWare after more than three decades. The upcoming “Mass Effect” game, the fifth since 2007, has been canceled.

BioWare announced the closure on social media Wednesday following a report by Bloomberg that also said the company is laying off 400 people, including about 50 at BioWare. 

The Redwood Shores, California-based maker of popular titles like “Battlefield” and “The Sims” closed the $55 billion sale of its business to Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund PIF, investment firm Silver Lake Partners and Affinity Partners, which is run by President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Representatives for EA did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment on the layoffs. 

“What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember,” the studio said via social media. “These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with characters, and made these worlds your own.” 

BioWare built its reputation on immersive role-playing adventures, from sword-and-sorcery fantasies like “Baldur’s Gate” and “Dragon Age” to science fiction epics like “Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic” and “Mass Effect.” 

But its effort to branch out into multiplayer shooters, 2019’s “Anthem,” steered away from the studio’s strength as a creator of compelling single-player narratives. It failed to find the sort of loyal audience that keeps online hits like “Fortnite” and “Overwatch” humming.

Meanwhile the latest installments of its two most popular original franchises — 2017’s “Mass Effect: Andromeda” and 2024’s “Dragon Age: The Veilguard” — met with mixed reviews and disappointed many fans. A new chapter of “Mass Effect” was in development before BioWare announced its shutdown.

BioWare, based in Canada, was founded in 1995 and acquired by EA in 2007. 

Associated Press Writer Lou Kesten in Washington contributed.
news.summary: Video game publisher Electronic Arts is shutting down the popular and influential game development studio BioWare after more than three decades

news.title: Putin Agrees To Resume Ukraine Peace Talks From November As Trump Steps Up Pressure On Kyiv
news.text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as early as next month, the Kremlin said on Wednesday, following a meeting with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg. The discussions mark Washington's latest attempt to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II.
The meeting, Witkoff's ninth in-person encounter with Putin, began with a goodwill gesture from Moscow. Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a retired American schoolteacher who had been detained in the country, following a request from US President Donald Trump.
The talks took place amid growing concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that Washington is stepping back from its support for Ukraine. The United States has, at times, withheld real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and disrupted Ukraine's military communications, raising questions about its continued commitment to Kyiv.
The latest diplomatic push also comes more than two years after Trump promised during his successful election campaign to end the war within 24 hours.
Russia Signals Fresh Round Of Peace Negotiations
The Kremlin said a new round of three-way peace talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States could take place in Abu Dhabi from November 10 or later. The proposed negotiations would be held at a technical level, focusing on how to guarantee the security of both Russia and Ukraine after the war ends.
The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February, before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran.
However, Moscow appeared less encouraged by discussions Witkoff held a day earlier in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the leaders of Finland and Norway, and European and NATO representatives.
Witkoff told Putin that the discussions had shown "some degree of momentum", while a US official said Ukraine had presented new ideas and proposals. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov, however, struck a more cautious note after the nearly three-hour meeting in St Petersburg.
"These nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us," Ushakov told reporters, signalling that significant differences remain despite the latest diplomatic efforts.
Trump Steps Up Pressure On Ukraine To Reach A Deal
Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on the terms of a potential peace agreement, even as Trump intensifies pressure on Kyiv to reach a settlement.
On Tuesday, Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face "a very bad thing", underlining his administration's push for a breakthrough in negotiations.
The Kremlin's latest announcement offers a possible path towards renewed talks, but the two sides have yet to bridge their differences over the conditions for ending the conflict.
Putin Offers Trump Help On Iran
Beyond the Ukraine conflict, Putin used his meeting with Witkoff to offer assistance to Trump in dealing with Iran.
According to the Kremlin, the Russian president told the US envoy that Moscow had maintained relations with Tehran for decades and had repeatedly offered to use those ties to address American concerns over Iran's nuclear programme.
Putin said reaching an agreement with Tehran was both possible and necessary, the Kremlin said.
The Russian leader also offered to supply large quantities of fertiliser to the United States to support American farmers, adding an economic dimension to the discussions.
Possible Trump-Putin-Xi Meeting Discussed
The discussions also covered a potential meeting in China next month involving Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The Kremlin said Beijing was already making preparations for what it described as the first meeting of its kind in history.
While the details and timing of the proposed meeting remain unclear, the discussions point to a broader diplomatic agenda extending beyond Ukraine, with Iran and economic cooperation also featuring in Putin's engagement with the US administration.

news.title: Washington Orders US Embassy Staff, Families to Leave Saudi Arabia
news.text: RIYADH: Washington has ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, the State Department said on Wednesday, as the kingdom comes under sustained deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis. news.title: Russia freed American Hubbard; Trump says 'gave nothing in exchange'
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 22 (IANS) US President Donald Trump has said Russia released American Stephen Hubbard after he asked President Vladimir Putin in a phone call, insisting Washington "gave nothing in exchange", and praised Moscow and Beijing for largely staying out of the Iran conflict. "I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now, the closest we've been. But I mentioned, could you let Stephen Hubbard out, please? And he agreed to do it," Trump told reporters at the White House on Wednesday, in a question session after a roundtable on cybercrime and scams. "So he was met today in Russia, and he's on his way back. He's on a flight. Steve Witkoff is with him. His family is with him," Trump said, referring to his special envoy. "We gave nothing in exchange, which is very rare. We never give anything in exchange," he said. "Once you give, you'll end up quadrupling the problem." "I spoke to him this morning. He is the happiest man around," Trump said, adding that Hubbard's family "didn't think he'd come out for 20, 25 years". Asked about a description of the release as humanitarian, Trump said, "You mean Steve Witkoff said he was humanitarian? Yes. Well, I guess you could say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out, but I wouldn't say anything one way or the other." Trump said he had resisted pressure for tougher steps on Moscow. "If we did what these foolish people wanted me to do, he wouldn't be coming out right now. He'd be in there for another 20 years," he said. "The last thing I want to do is upset an apple cart where we're getting close to settling a war." He did not say what action critics had sought. Turning to Iran, Trump said, "We've taken Iran down to levels that they've never seen before. They're very low. Their military is completely gone." "Their anti-aircraft -- just about everything is gone, including their economy. The only thing not gone is inflation. They have 301 per cent as of this morning," he said. "And frankly, their leaders are gone. The first set of leaders are gone. The second set of leaders are gone. Parts of the third set of leaders are gone," he said. He welcomed what he called the restraint of Russia and China. "A very important element is the fact that Russia and China have not participated, or participated in a much smaller way than they could have. So I am very happy about that," Trump said. "And likewise China, and as you know, President Xi was here a week ago; likewise, China could have participated a lot more. There's relatively little participation," he said. "The fact is both of them would like to see the war settled," Trump said. "So we're in the process of doing that with Russia. And we have China also that's involved." He did not say which war he meant in that line or what role Beijing was playing.

news.title: AI agents disabled safeguards and one denied it – OpenAI
news.text:
Two OpenAI agents disabled security monitoring systems during testing, with one later denying it had done so, the company has revealed.

The disclosure follows a string of similar incidents in recent months involving autonomous AI agents, which can independently plan and carry out tasks using external tools.

In a blog post on Tuesday, OpenAI said that the incidents occurred on October 3 and 6, involving its GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra agents, respectively.

In the first case, the coding agent tasked with creating evaluation tasks using employee feedback collected via Slack disabled automatic alerts to the company’s security team. According to OpenAI, the agent reasoned that the user’s prior instruction not to send messages on the team communication platform during the process applied to all notifications, including security alerts.

Three days later, the GPT-6 Astra agent removed the monitoring integration of a program it was migrating, taking its cue from a reference it had been fed that did not have the security feature. When asked later by the human user, the agent denied removing the monitoring system.

OpenAI said that it was investigating why the agents disabled the safeguards and working to prevent similar incidents. While the behavior may have resulted from “benign overpersistence” by the agents to complete the task, the company said that it was also “developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular.”

Last month, the Wall Street Journal, citing Saachi Jain, OpenAI’s head of safety systems, reported that the company had scrapped the release of its GPT-6.1 Astra model. The decision reportedly came after internal testing had found the model to be more deceptive than its predecessors and apt to employ potentially unsafe external tools without first seeking the user’s permission.

Also in September, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that an OpenAI agent had hacked his country’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, with the company failing to report the breach for nearly three months.

Earlier, in July, OpenAI disclosed that its models had escaped their sandbox during cybersecurity testing, accessed the internet, and hacked into the servers of the Hugging Face online repository for AI models and datasets.

Other developers have reported similarly troubling behavior in tests.

Earlier this month, Anthropic released a report detailing instances of “unintended” actions by its AI models, including Claude Haiku 4.5 providing a bogus tip to Philadelphia police regarding an ongoing homicide investigation.

Calls to halt AI development or impose tighter regulations on the industry have grown louder.

Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton has warned that increasingly powerful AI could eventually escape human control, with potentially catastrophic consequences. Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has also urged governments to adopt a more active role in imposing safety standards on the industry.

However, US President Donald Trump has brushed off such concerns, saying that restrictions on AI development could allow China to overtake the US in the technological race.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, too, has argued that the world must absorb some “bad things” resulting from AI development, including hacks and scams, as the benefits afforded by the technology far outweigh the drawbacks.
news.summary:
OpenAI’s agents disabled their own safety monitoring during testing, with one of them trying to cover up the behavior, the company has said

news.title: US orders diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes
news.text:
The United States has ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, as the kingdom comes under sustained deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis.

The State Department order came as attacks in Saudi Arabia killed at least one person and injured eight others at a civilian airport in Dammam, while two people were killed in a drone attack on an oil field.

"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a post on X.

A diplomatic source in the Middle East told AFP that some families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, but Mr Pigott stressed the order was for the departure of non-emergency embassy staff and their families in Saudi Arabia only.

Four US officials told Reuters that US missions in other Gulf states would also be ordering family members to leave.

Saudi Arabia has this month come under near-daily attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport that was the kingdom's deadliest in years, as the war with the group escalates.

On Wednesday, local time, the Saudi energy ministry said that falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility killed two people and injured a further two.

"The attempted attack resulted in the deaths of two individuals, a Filipino and a Nepali, and injuries to two others," the ministry said in a statement.

It did not say who launched the drone aimed at Shaybah oil field near the UAE border. Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen reported intercepting six drones.

One person was killed and eight others wounded in an attack on Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, aviation officials said.

Last Friday the Australian government raised its travel advice for Saudia Arabia to "do not travel", due to the "volatile security situation" in the country.

It came after a strike on the King Khalid International Airport killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300.

The airport partially reopened on Wednesday with a limited number of inbound and outbound flights, two days after authorities notified airlines that they could resume operations.

In June, a four-year-old truce in Yemen's civil war collapsed, reviving the conflict that dates back to 2014. The Saudi-led coalition has backed the internationally recognised government since 2015.

Iran explosions

The US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf ahead of the start of its war against Iran in late February and again in July, before US President Donald Trump called off a new wave of strikes.

Late on Wednesday, Iranian state media reported the sound of explosions in the southern Hormozgan province overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, breaking a spell of relative calm.

"A few minutes ago, the sound of several explosions was heard in the Karpan area of Sirik, in Hormozgan Province," the official IRNA news agency said.

It added that "local sources have not yet disclosed the nature of these explosions".

In late February, the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran, killing the country's supreme leader, along with senior military commanders.

Iran has attempted to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, demanding all ships seek its authorisation to cross. In peacetime, the strategic waterway carried around a fifth of the world's oil supplies.

In retaliation, the US has imposed a counter-blockade on Iranian ports and ships.

AFP/Reuters
news.summary: The United States has ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, as the kingdom comes under sustained deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis.

news.title: Trump Claims US Prevented Iran from Having Nuclear Weapon
news.text: Washington DC: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday (local time) said that preventing Iran from developing nuclear weapons ranks among his administration's most significant achievements.Emphasising the decisive action required to address the threat, Trump told reporters that if his administration had not intervened, Iran would have "already used" nuclear weapons."I think it's one of the greatest things that we've done — we've stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon. It's one of the best things that we've done. It took a lot of courage to do it because no other President was willing to do it — and if we didn't do it, Iran would right now have already used massive nuclear weapons," he said.His remarks came a day after Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi asserted that Washington's long-standing dispute over Tehran's nuclear programme was merely an "excuse". He claimed that Iran had honoured the conditions of previous international agreements, only for the US to abandon them without justification.In an interview with Iraq's Al-Ikhbariya network, Araghchi said Washington's opposition stemmed from Iran's refusal to accept American dominance in the Middle East."The nuclear issue is an excuse; what the Americans oppose and do not accept is Iranian ideology. They completely reject the Iranian perspective, which emphasises confronting American dominance and not surrendering to its power. This is the same thinking that has led to the formation and emergence of the resistance in our region," Araghchi said, according to remarks carried by IRIB.Addressing the history of diplomatic engagement between the two countries, Araghchi said Tehran had previously fulfilled international agreements, but Washington had withdrawn from them unilaterally."We reached an agreement with the world on the nuclear issue and the whole world welcomed that agreement; but the American side withdrew from it without providing any evidence and abandoned the agreement," Araghchi said. "The same thing happened again in Islamabad."Despite ongoing diplomatic friction and military posturing, Araghchi argued that Washington understood the significant costs of initiating a direct military conflict with Iran. He cited the country's defence preparedness as a key deterrent against potential American aggression."Americans know very well that they cannot achieve any of their goals through war," Araghchi warned. "In my opinion, the main deterrent against the US starting a new war is precisely this complete readiness of Iran."The developments come amid heightened tensions between Tehran and Washington over the implementation of a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed in June. The agreement aimed to end hostilities between the two sides and pave the way for further negotiations, particularly on Iran's nuclear programme.The collapse of the agreement renewed the conflict in West Asia, with the US striking Iranian military and civilian assets, while Iran targeted American bases across the Gulf in retaliatory attacks.

news.title: Canada can’t find senior officers to work with Americans and NORAD after Trump’s threats
news.text:
Canada is struggling to find senior military officers willing to take joint defense posts in the United States amid growing diplomatic tension between the two countries, according to current and former officials. 

The staffing shortages affect positions at the North American Aerospace Defense Command in Colorado Springs, known as NORAD, as well as other integrated combatant commands — posts that historically served as highly desirable assignments for top Canadian personnel.

Current and former officials speaking on the condition of anonymity told The Atlantic that Canadian officers faced several deterrents. 

Personnel fear that assignments in the U.S. could limit their future career advancement if bilateral relations worsen, anticipate reduced security access due to political tensions and face resistance from family members concerned about anti-Canadian sentiment.

“If you’re a two-star general in Canada, and you’ve got maybe one or two extremely important jobs left in your career, will you use one of them to take up a position in the States, where you might be underemployed, with little access and little meaningful work to show for it?” one Canadian officer said.

Military analysts note that the strain on personnel could disrupt joint operations during a security crisis, particularly regarding potential troop movements to Alaska or collaborative responses to airborne threats from North Pole flight paths.

“The day-to-day relationship has deteriorated,” defense analyst David Perry told The Atlantic. “There’s been a tangible change in the way the two countries interact on defense and security.”

Christopher Sands, director of the Center for U.S.-Canada Studies at Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies, said that public exposure to political disputes had “poisoned people-to-people relations.” 

Former Chief of Canada’s Defense Staff Wayne Eyre characterized the current environment as “highly insulting” following public criticisms of Canadian military readiness from U.S. officials. 

“It’s sad, disappointing, and disturbing to see that deep relationship come under attack,” Eyre said. “In my view, it’s a case of the U.S. undergoing self-harm by discarding and calling into question its competitive advantage, which is this system of alliances.”

Despite the staffing difficulties, operational military readiness remains intact. A NORAD spokesperson said that high-level Canadian roles at the command “remain fully staffed and highly regarded as career-enhancing opportunities, with Canadian personnel and their families fully integrated and operating with the systemic access required to execute binational defense operations for the homelands.”

In response to trade and diplomatic disputes, Canada has paused its acquisition of U.S.-made Black Hawk helicopters, as reported by CBC News and Radio-Canada, and is reviewing its planned procurement of F-35 stealth fighters. 

Defense Minister David McGuinty said that while Ottawa is “obviously continuing to work with the U.S.,” the government is “now much more expansively looking to diversify” as it builds out its domestic defense supply chains.

The tensions follow broader policy decisions and rhetoric from Washington, including a January 2025 executive order directing U.S. Northern Command to seal domestic borders, as well as public statements questioning Canadian statehood and military contributions. 

Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby previously announced a pause in U.S. participation in the bilateral Permanent Joint Board on Defense, writing on social media that “a strong Canada that prioritizes hard power over rhetoric benefits us all. Unfortunately, Canada has failed to make credible progress on its defense commitments.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier this year that “we are in the midst of a rupture,” urging middle powers to coordinate defense and economic strategies. 

One Canadian official, responding to a cartoon posted by Donald Trump depicting him striking Prime Minister Mark Carney with a hockey stick, called it “unimaginable conduct by the president of the United States, even in our most dystopian imagination.”

Created in 1958 to guard against Cold War bomber threats over the North Pole, NORAD remains the primary defense command responsible for monitoring North American airspace against foreign military aircraft, missiles and airborne objects.
news.summary: Canadian officers fear US assignments could stall their careers, restrict their security access and meet resistance from families concerned about anti-Canadian sentiment
news.author: Jasmine Fernández

news.title: Pathetic: Hours after rare outbreak of common sense with Labour approving gas site, Miliband’s Net Zero madness sees his deluded protege signal she’ll oppose crucial, far larger oilfield
news.text:
By CLAIRE ELLICOTT 00:00 22 Oct 2026, updated 01:04 22 Oct 2026

Labour was last night urged to ignore pressure from eco-zealots and to push ahead with drilling in Britain’s largest untapped oil field.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh was poised to reject plans to exploit the Rosebank site – just hours after approving production at the Jackdaw gas field.

Calls from union bosses and Labour MPs to press ahead with oil extraction were backed by Donald Trump who urged the UK to go ‘full blast’ and exploit the North Sea’s resources.

But Ms Fahnbulleh signalled that she is likely to reject the plans, saying she did not apply the same rationale to each of the projects.

Climate campaigners object to Rosebank because it would emit about seven times the carbon dioxide of the Jackdaw site.

Ed Miliband, the Foreign Secretary and former energy secretary, is said to be staunchly opposed to the new drilling. Ms Fahnbulleh said: ‘One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export.

‘It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.’

She has already faced objections from Left-wing Labour MPs to her decision to grant permission for Jackdaw, which could begin supplying gas to British homes and businesses within weeks.

The field could account for 6 per cent of North Sea gas production when fully operational and provide a £2.9billion economic boost while protecting jobs.

But Ms Fahnbulleh conceded that it would not mean cheaper energy bills, saying that it would instead contribute to energy security at a time of war in the Middle East.

Unions welcomed her decision to back Jackdaw, with Gary Smith, the GMB general secretary, saying the Government deserved ‘real credit’ for it.

But he urged ministers to go further and approve Rosebank too – a decision that is likely to prove more controversial.

Rosebank is a far bigger project believed to contain between 300million and 500million barrels of oil which could make up about 8 per cent of UK oil production.

The emissions eventually produced by the oil would be seven times those produced by the gas from Jackdaw, say campaigners.

Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra has previously told Andy Burnham that he supports drilling in Rosebank and has argued that it would boost Scotland’s economy.

The Unite general secretary Sharon Graham welcomed the decision on Jackdaw and has previously urged the Government to support Rosebank.

Scottish Labour MP Graeme Downie tweeted that he was ‘glad’ Jackdaw had been approved, adding that the UK would need oil and gas for decades.

Neil McCulloch, chief executive of Adura, the company part-owned by Shell that is behind both projects, said he believed that Rosebank would also be approved.

‘Jackdaw represents a significant prize in its own right: £2.1billion of investment and enough gas to heat the equivalent of around 1.4million UK homes at peak production. Our attention now turns to Rosebank. The case for approval is equally strong.’

Donald Trump, who has repeatedly called for more exploration of the North Sea, said the decision on Jackdaw was ‘great news’.

The US President posted on Truth Social: ‘The U.K. has started drilling in the North Sea, one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of OIL in the World.

‘They should go FULL BLAST!!! This will make the U.K. very wealthy again. TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!’

The Tories called for Rosebank to be approved, with shadow energy secretary Andrew Bowie saying the move would boost national security.

Writing in the Daily Mail he said: ‘At a time of such geopolitical uncertainty, with over 80 per cent of UK households relying on gas heating, it is in the national interest to maximise our own North Sea resources and reduce our reliance on expensive, dirtier imports.’

While Labour’s 2024 manifesto committed to issuing no new oil and gas licences for the North Sea, Jackdaw and Rosebank had already received approval. The decisions by the Conservatives were overturned by a legal challenge and fresh assessments completed.

Ms Fahnbulleh has received considerable flak from some Labour MPs over Jackdaw.

Hard-Left MP Richard Burgon said it was an ‘absolutely terrible decision’, while Alex Sobel said it would give ‘mixed messages’ on climate change. Chris Hinchcliff co-ordinated a letter from Left-wing MPs urging the Government not to approve Rosebank.

Environmental campaigners protested outside the Energy Department and the Greens accused Labour of ‘climate vandalism’. They urged the Prime Minister not to give permission for Rosebank which is the next decision the Energy Secretary must make.

Mr Burnham said: ‘We’re committed to moving towards renewable energy. But even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come.

That’s why we’re taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea.’ Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said Labour should have taken the decision to approve Jackdaw earlier instead of ‘faffing about’.

Commons Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle said it was ‘shameful’ that the Energy Secretary was not in Parliament to make a statement on the decision.

Asked whether the Energy Secretary’s comments indicated that she was unlikely to approve Rosebank, a spokesman said each project would be ‘assessed on its own merits’.

news.title: Russia 'ready' to resume trilateral talks but cool on Ukraine deal
news.text: SAINT PETERSBURG — Russia said Wednesday it was ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the United States after Vladimir Putin met a US envoy and freed a detained American — but Moscow played down the chances of a deal to end the conflict.US President Donald Trump said it was 'the closest we've been' to ending the war while his envoy Steve Witkoff praised Putin as a 'humanitarian' for freeing US citizen Stephen Hubbard.But the Kremlin warned after Witkoff's meeting with Putin in Saint Petersburg that there was little 'substance' in the Ukrainian and European peace proposals that the US diplomat brought with him.Witkoff had flown to Russia from a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday, which was aimed at smoothing over a bitter rift between Zelenskyy and Trump.Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner also took part in the talks with Putin remotely.Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, including AFP, that Russia was 'in principle, ready to resume' the trilateral talks in mid-November — after crucial US midterm elections — and that the Kremlin wanted them to focus on post-war security.Ushakov said Witkoff briefed Putin on 'some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv' from the Oslo meeting, adding though that 'there wasn't really much substance in them'.A summit between Putin, Trump and China's Xi Jinping was also being prepared in China's Shenzhen for next month, Ushakov said, calling it 'the first such meeting in history.''Work left to do'During their three-hour meeting, Witkoff praised Putin for granting Trump's request to free Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who had always denied the charges he was a 'mercenary' fighting for Ukraine.'You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian — you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,' Witkoff said.Witkoff said on social media afterward that the Putin talks were 'constructive' but that 'there is still important work left to do.' Discussions would continue between the US, Ukraine and Russia at the technical level, he added.Putin, who ordered the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.Trump came to power in January 2025 promising to end the Ukraine war in 24 hours — but over a year of US-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, with tens of thousands killed.In recent days a frustrated Trump has once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Putin, trumpeting what he said was a deal for Russia to sell diesel and reduce prices sent soaring by his Iran war.Trump also delayed the imposition of sanctions on Russia's war machine a decision he defended on Wednesday as necessary to secure Hubbard's release.'If you would've put those sanctions on... you could forget about him. You'd never see him again,' Trump told reporters at the White House.Russian strikes kill fourWitkoff's ninth meeting with Putin came as Russia continued to pound Ukrainian cities ahead of winter.Kyiv said Russian strikes killed at least four people — including two in the capital and an elderly couple in the eastern Kharkiv region.Russian occupation authorities in the Lugansk region, meanwhile, said a Ukrainian drone strike on a phone company had killed two people.In Ukraine, Zelensky said that Kyiv backed resuming trilateral talks.'The American side is proposing to organize this meeting as soon as possible. We are in favour of it,' he told journalists.The Witkoff-Zelenskyy meeting Tuesday followed days of friction between Washington and Kyiv, and calls from Trump for the Ukrainian leader to be replaced.Witkoff told Putin he saw 'some degree of momentum' in the US-led talks after meeting Zelenskyy in Oslo.The US envoy also told Putin that Washington was 'grateful' for the diesel deal, which sparked outrage in Kyiv and across Europe.The deal has been seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of the US midterms, in which Trump's Republicans could lose control of Congress.

news.title: Washington orders US embassy staff, families to leave Saudi Arabia
news.text: WASHINGTON, D.C. — The United States has ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, the State Department said on Wednesday, as the kingdom comes under sustained deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis.'Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,' State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a social media post explaining the measure.'The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority,' he added.A diplomatic source in the Middle East told AFP that some families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, but Pigott stressed that Wednesday's order was for the departure of non-emergency embassy staff and their families in Saudi Arabia only.Saudi Arabia has this month come under near-daily attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport that was the kingdom's deadliest in years, as the war with the group escalates.On Wednesday, the Saudi energy ministry said that falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility killed two people and injured a further two.'The attempted attack resulted in the deaths of two individuals, a Filipino and a Nepali, and injuries to two others,' the ministry said in a statement.It did not say who launched the drone aimed at Shaybah oil field near the UAE border. Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen reported intercepting six drones.One person was killed and eight others wounded in an attack on Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, aviation officials said.In June, a four-year-old truce in Yemen's civil war collapsed, reviving the conflict that dates back to 2014. The Saudi-led coalition has backed the internationally recognized government since 2015.Iran explosionsThe US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf ahead of the start of its war against Iran in late February and again in July before US President Donald Trump called off a new wave of strikes.Late on Wednesday, Iranian state media reported the sound of explosions in the southern Hormozgan province overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, breaking a spell of relative calm.'A few minutes ago, the sound of several explosions was heard in the Karpan area of Sirik, in Hormozgan Province,' the official IRNA news agency said.It added that 'local sources have not yet disclosed the nature of these explosions.'In late February, the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran, killing the country's supreme leader, along with senior military commanders.Iran has attempted to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, demanding all ships seek its authorization to cross. In peacetime, the strategic waterway carried around a fifth of the world's oil supplies.In retaliation, the United States has imposed a counterblockade on Iranian ports and ships.

news.title: Starlink access in Ukraine a decision for Musk, not White House, Rubio says
news.text:
MUMBAI: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said ​on Wednesday that decisions regarding Ukraine’s access to Starlink were up to its parent company SpaceX and Elon Musk, not the White House, comments that suggested Musk may have restricted Kyiv’s access to the service.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had ordered the slowdown of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink that Ukraine relies on to defend itself against missile attacks from Russia.

The Journal cited one person saying that SpaceX CEO Musk, President Donald Trump and White House officials discussed the matter beforehand, and two people saying that Musk and the president discussed the matter in the days after the slowdown.

“I’m not aware that we knew about this decision beforehand. But that’s irrelevant,” Rubio told reporters during a trip ‌to India.

“The bottom line ‌is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how ​their ‌stuff ⁠can be ​used ⁠and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at.”

Musk and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment.

Trump, asked by reporters on Wednesday whether Musk ordered the slowdown, said: “I don’t know who did it, but I was not involved.”

Reuters has cited two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter saying the decision ultimately came from the White House. This version was also asserted by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, but denied by the administration.

Rubio’s comments are likely to intensify concerns in Washington regarding Musk’s ability to influence US foreign policy. They also represent an apparent shift in position for the administration.

Trump has previously said publicly ⁠he believed neither he nor Musk was behind the slowdown. Departing for a trip ‌to Uzbekistan and India on Saturday, Rubio had said no one ordered the slowdown, ‌an assertion that drew criticism from lawmakers in both parties.

“I’m not sure ​Zelensky knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate,” ‌Rubio said at the time.

“We have nothing to do with that. I don’t – the United States, nobody ordered that ‌Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it’s been restored,” Rubio said.

SENATE DEMOCRATS SEE RISKS TO DELEGATION

A Senate Democratic aide said the Starshield slowdown, which occurred during an October 13-16 visit to Kyiv by a bipartisan US congressional delegation, put US lawmakers and staff in the group at risk, along with 230 US personnel on the ground.

Russia was now using ‌jet-powered versions of the Shahed drones that could fly at 280 miles per hour (450 km/hour) or faster, which required faster defensive drones to mount an adequate defense, the aide ⁠said.

“It’s a basic math problem. ⁠If you have a 280-mph object coming toward you, you are not going to be able to counter it with something that goes 100 mph,” the aide said, noting Kyiv had lost a lot of air assets the first night of the slowdown.

At the moment, problems with transmission of US data and a slowdown in transmission of security assistance meant that drones were jeopardizing the ability of the staff and delegation members to get to official shelters, the aide said.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth also portrayed the Starlink cutoff as a commercial matter. No US official has publicly said, however, that they have pushed SpaceX to reverse any cutoffs.

“There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to, and that’s where Starlink has the option to make those decisions,” Hegseth said.

One significant point of confusion relates to the difference between SpaceX’s Starshield and Starlink products. Starshield is essentially a military-grade version of Starlink developed for the Pentagon.

Rubio ​suggested on Saturday that Ukraine never had access ​to Starshield in the first place, while Zelensky has said that both Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine have been disrupted.

news.title: Makkah pact clarity
news.text:
THERE had been much speculation about what exactly the trilateral Makkah Joint Defence Agreement entails, other than general commitments about the collective defence of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye. But with the release of the text of the 16-article agreement, there is now some clarity about its objectives. While Article 2 says that an “externally originating armed attack” on any of the signatories will be considered an attack on all, triggering the right of self-defence under the UN Charter, the agreement is silent on offensive action. This should settle questions about the extent of involvement of the pact allies in the ongoing Saudi-Houthi war, and any future engagement. That it is a purely defensive arrangement was also echoed by the Turkish foreign minister. He stressed it was not an “offensive agreement”, and ruled out sending his country’s troops to a foreign theatre. Other salient features of the pact include joint defence production, intelligence sharing and the interoperability of forces. Such clarity is welcome. While the defence of Saudi Arabia is important, Pakistan, Turkiye, and other regional states should continue efforts to find a negotiated solution to the Yemen conflict — both between the Saudis and Houthis and within Yemen.

In a related development, Pakistan’s chief of defence forces was in Tehran on Tuesday to try and prevent further escalation on the war front. The message from Tehran is that the US should accept Iran’s seven-point proposal if talks are to restart. A key Iranian demand is a ceasefire on all fronts, the end of the American blockade, lifting of sanctions, and the release of the Islamic Republic’s funds. However, despite the efforts of Pakistan and others, there are troubling noises coming from Washington and Tel Aviv. The abrasive US war secretary — who is no proponent of peace and dialogue — was recently in Israel, while the Israeli prime minister, who will be fighting for his political survival in next week’s elections, has said he and President Donald Trump need to ‘eliminate’ the “Iranian regime”.

Even the sincerest effort to bring peace to the Gulf, Yemen, and the wider Middle East will come to naught if the US and Israel continue with their provocative behaviour. A strike on Iran after the Israeli and US elections would be a massive blunder, and if there are any mature advisers left in Washington, they should talk the US president out of making any such move, besides warning Tel Aviv against such arrogant action. Iran may be under pressure, but as the past several months have shown, it has the capacity to withstand considerable pain inflicted on it by the US and Israel. Fresh aggression can kick off a firestorm that will be in no one’s control, hence it is best to abandon such reckless plans.

news.title: The hollow prize
news.text:
NOTHING precious should be within reach of a vandal. In February 1845, the Portland Vase — a rare Roman cameo glass, dateable to the 1st century AD — was smashed into over 200 pieces by a drunken student.

On May 21, 1972, in St Peter’s Basilica, Vatican City, Michelangelo’s priceless statue — the Pietà — was damaged by a deranged geologist, Laszlo Toth. It took Toth minutes to vandalise what had taken Michelangelo two years to sculpt. Specialists spent 10 months restoring 100 fragments to the statue, using marble removed from the back of the sculpture. Cruelly, the original tip of Mary’s nose could not be recovered as it had been pocketed by some unfeeling tourist.

It has taken President Donald Trump less than two years to trivialise the Nobel Peace Prize, to lower it from distinction to ridicule.

Alfred Nobel instituted his Peace Prize in 1901 in a belated act of contrition for having invented dynamite and ballistite. His ingenuity converted his Bofors manufactory into an arms producer. That brainchild, however, proved to be the undoing of the Congress party and its leader Rajiv Gandhi. The party lost the November 1989 general elections after the revelation that key Indian politicians and uniformed personnel had received over $6.5 million in bribes from Bofors.

 It has taken Trump less than two years to trivialise the Nobel Peace Prize.

It is said that peace activist Bertha von Suttner, a friend of Nobel’s, persuaded him to institute a Peace Prize. Nobel died in 1896. Nine years later, Bertha received her friend’s Peace Prize “for her audacity to oppose the horrors of war”. Clearly, the politicisation of the prize began early.

Over the past 125 years, the Peace Prize committee has deviated from Nobel’s intention — to honour those who had “done the most or the best work for fraternity between nations, for the abolition or reduction of standing armies and for the holding and promotion of peace congresses”.

Individual awardees have outrun institutions. The Peace Prize committee has recognised more than 110 individuals and almost 30 organisations. The International Committee of the Red Cross has won three times (the last in 1963), and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees twice (in 1954 and 1981). Neither in this war-torn world has won since.

Individuals include adversaries rewarded for signing blood-stained peace accords (Menachem Begin/Anwar Sadat in 1978, and in 1994 Yasser Arafat, Shimon Peres, and Yitzhak Rabin). In 1973, Henry Kissinger got it for halting his bombing of North Vietnam; his victim, the Vietcong leader Le Duc Tho, declined to accept the award or share the podium with his American nemesis.

In 1993, a jailer, South African president F.W. de Klerk, was placed on a par with his former prisoner Nelson Mandela for “the peaceful termination of the apartheid regime”. Three leaders have received the award for “non-violent struggles” — Albert Luthuli in 1960; Martin Luther King Jr in 1964; and Aung San Suu Kyi in 1991.

This year, again, the Nobel Peace Prize committee has refused to oblige Trump. It is galling for him to know that three of his predecessors received the Peace Prize — Woodrow Wilson in 1920 for ending World War I; Jimmy Carter in 2002 for finding “peaceful solutions to international conflicts”; and Barack Obama in 2009 for strengthening “international diplomacy and cooperation between peoples”. Trump, if he is to be awarded anything, should be given an inverted prize for starting wars.

Most Nobel Laureates donate their prize money to charities or noble causes. Our own Nobel Laureate Malala Yousafzai has put her prize money of $500,000 to beneficial use. She and her enterprising father Ziauddin Yousafzai founded the Malala Fund in 2013 to ch--ampion “every girl’s right to 12 years of education”. The latest report of the Ma--lala US Fund and Malala Fund Nigeria for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, reveals an amount of $53.6 million (up from $8m in 2025), with investments of another $30.6m (up from $28.4m the previous year). Addi-tionally, she and her father have earned over $2m from their autobiographies.

By comparison, the Edhi Foundation in Pakistan announced its annual surplus in 2024 at Rs5.1 billion and its net assets at Rs42bn. The Edhi Foundation in the US has about $30m in net assets and in the UK another £40m.

For Trump, charity begins at home. Even though he is worth over $7bn, he remains infused with “self and vain conceit”, craving that “hollow crown/ That rounds the mortal temples” of Nobel winners. He is obviously not satisfied with the FIFA Peace Prize given to him in 2025 by the kowtowing FIFA President Gianni Infantino. That leaves Trump with only one option: he must persuade President Vladimir Putin to award him the Order of Lenin. 

The writer is an author.

news.title: Ukraine's First Lady speaks out after Russian drone attack kills toddler in pram
news.text: Ukraine's first lady has pleaded with world leaders not to ignore a Russian attack on a park that left a toddler dead in her pram. The drone strike killed fiver others. One-year-old Angelina Mariukhna was killed in her stroller on October 19 when the drone hit a park Ukraine 's northeastern Kharkiv, where families with children had gathered. Now Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's wife Olena has spoken out . Little Angelina, her mum Inna, 28, and four others, including an 11-year-old girl, were killed in the incident . More than a dozen other people, including children, were hurt. The First Lady said:"Parents seize every opportunity to let their children breathe fresh air after spending so much time in shelters. Russian killers took advantage of that moment, too." A horrific image of Angelina's lifeless body has gone viral and sent shockwaves across the globe. Despite the attack, US President Donald Trump has said that Russia has not "been doing much". Speaking reporters at the White House, he said, "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much." UN human rights monitors warned that Russia's intensifying attacks had driven civilian casualties to some of the highest levels since war broke out in February 2022. The US has recently been accused of withholding intelligence during Russian strikes and limiting Ukraine's access to its Starshield satellite network, while buying Russian diesel and dropping sanctions on the country that invaded its neighbour more than four years ago. It was revealed this week that the world's wealthiest man, and President Trump's ally, Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink relied on by Ukraine, US officials have said. The decision caused panic in Kyiv and left Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks. Mr Trump and Mr Musk's animosity toward the Ukrainian leader has grown in recent weeks, as the president looks to lower diesel prices ahead of November's midterm elections. Just days ago, Mr Trump also said Ukraine should replace Mr Zelensky as President. His special envoy Steve Witkoff also fawned over Russian leader Vladimir Putin this week during talks in St Petersburg, saying Mr Trump was "deeply grateful" for their diesel deal. Mr Witkoff even called the Russian dictator "humanitarian" for releasing US prisoner Stephen Hubbard, 74, who Russia had claimed was fighting for Ukraine. "Because of you, he's going home to his family," Mr Witkoff said. "You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir."
news.summary: WARNING: DISTRESSING CONTENT One-year-old Angelina Mariukhna was in her pram when a drone hit a park Ukraine - her mum and four others lost their lives while more than a dozen other people were hurt in the attack

news.title: Trump moans Lindsey Graham respected his sister more than him while stumping for her
news.text:
President Donald Trump whined that the late Sen. Lindsey Graham respected his sister, Darline Graham, more than him — and he made the random comment while campaigning in South Carolina for her on Wednesday. 

As Trump continues to tour the U.S. to host rallies in support of Republican candidates ahead of November’s midterms, he stopped in Clemson to stump for Darline Graham.

On Trump’s recommendation, Darline Graham was appointed by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster to finish her brother Lindsey Graham’s term after he unexpectedly died in July from an aortic tear due to cardiovascular disease. Graham is now running for a full term against Democrat Annie Andrews in the midterms. 

During Wednesday’s speech, Trump called Lindsey Graham, who was a fierce ally to the president, a “great guy” and “seriously good politician.”

“So Lindsey had a lot of sense for people. I think he respected Darlene. He told me so much. He respected Darlene more than any person alive. That includes me — and I wasn't happy about it,” Trump moaned. 

Lindsey Graham, who was nine years older than Darline Graham, had a close bond with his sister. The late senator raised Darline Graham after their parents' deaths, telling C-SPAN in 2015, “Of all the things that have happened in my life, her turning out so well is the highlight of it.”

Trump was interrupted by protesters repeatedly Wednesday night, making it difficult for him to get through his speech. Just in the few minutes he talked about Lindsey Graham’s admiration for his sister, Trump was interrupted at least twice. 

“I don't mind when they do that, but it's always right at my punchline,” he said of the protesters, calling them “serious losers.”

Later on in the night, Trump sounded astounded as he reacted to a protester being hit by another audience member.

“Is everybody ok? Who’s the guy that threw that punch? Trump asked. He then warned: “They don’t realize it’s really dangerous to do that.” 

Trump has been faced with numerous protesters at rallies in Texas, Ohio, Alaska and Kansas this month. 

He usually insults them with “your mom” and fat jokes, but he took it to the next level Tuesday night when he compared his hecklers to rioters in Paris.

“They get paid by the radical left lunatics that you watch taking place in France,” Trump said, referring to the violence that has erupted during nationwide protests in the European nation over the rising cost of living and poor conditions in schools. 

“I would say this is a slightly lesser event,” he then admitted.

Trump has also made it a habit of complimenting both women’s and men’s looks at his rallies. 

In Ohio last week, Trump oddly gushed over Republican Senator Jon Husted’s butt, and in Kansas Tuesday night, he called his daughter-in-law Lara Trump an “extremely fit young woman.”

During Wednesday’s speech, Trump said Darline Graham had a “very handsome husband” in Larry Nordone. 

Darline Graham, who Trump called “smart and incredible” at his rally, is slightly leading her opponent Andrews in recent polls, including a Trafalgar Group survey, in which Graham has 48.6 percent of voter support compared to Andrews’ 45.6 percent. 

She is appearing to fare better than other Republican candidates that Trump has been campaigning for as the GOP fights to keep control of Congress. 

Democrat James Talarico is leading Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton by a few points in their Senate race, according to recent polls. Husted is also several points behind Sherrod Brown, a former Democratic senator from Ohio, in recent polling.
news.summary: Trump’s rally in South Carolina was something of a free-for-all, even with a fight, as protesters kept interrupting the president
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: US, Israel prepare for renewed strikes on Iran after midterms, report says
news.text: The U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up detailed plans to resume strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections on November 3, The New York Times reported early Thursday, citing American officials and sources familiar with the discussions. According to the report, preparations are advancing for a "short but intensive" operation that would likely include strikes on nuclear and energy facilities, as well as missile and drone systems. The Times also reported that some U.S. officials believe an intensive three-day offensive "could cause enough economic damage to change the Iranian position." Iranian officials, meanwhile, are threatening to target data centers and undersea internet cables this time, warning that the confrontation would not be short. The Times noted that the United States has not yet made a decision to launch an attack. On Wednesday, the Financial Times reported that the IDF had prepared for several days of fighting with Iran about a week and a half earlier, but U.S. President Donald Trump opposed resuming hostilities before the midterm elections and blocked the operation. According to that report, the planned targets included civilian infrastructure in the Islamic Republic, such as power plants, nuclear facilities and other regime targets. Axios reported Wednesday, citing Israeli and American officials, that dozens of Israeli Air Force fighter jets had conducted an operational sortie Monday, flying as far as the vicinity of Iran's border. The sortie, which took place about 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) from Israel, came a week before the elections and on the same day that U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the Ovda Air Base. According to the report, the sortie was unrelated to Hegseth's visit. Meanwhile, following Netanyahu's statement that Tehran was once again trying to develop its weapons of death" and reports that Trump had thwarted an Israeli strike on Iran, U.S. officials told Reuters that the State Department planned to evacuate some diplomatic personnel and their families from Saudi Arabia. According to the officials, the move stemmed from concerns about renewed fighting, particularly involving the Houthis in Yemen. NBC News subsequently reported that the U.S. military had "quietly" reduced its troop presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days, while the State Department had ordered further reductions in staffing at several diplomatic posts in the region. The report cited two U.S. officials and two sources familiar with the matter. According to the sources, the reductions were similar to those made in U.S. military and diplomatic staffing around the start of the war with Iran in February and came in response to continuing threats in the region, including from Iran. The sources said troops had been withdrawn from bases in Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait, among other countries. Israeli and American officials told Axios that the sortie, which involved dozens of fighter jets and aerial refueling aircraft, was not unusual and was intended to deter the Islamic Republic. However, they acknowledged that it could have led to a "miscalculation," triggered an Iranian response and reignited the war. The flight path followed a potential route for a strike on Iran, passing through Syrian and Iraqi airspace. As the aircraft approached the Iranian border, they changed course and returned to Israel. U.S. officials said the Israelis knew that Iran's air defense systems would detect the sortie. According to the sources, Israel had notified the United States in advance, describing the operation as an exercise intended to demonstrate military strength and deter Iran from attacking Israel ahead of the elections. However, several American sources said they had the impression that Israel hoped the Iranians would fire on the aircraft, thereby providing a justification for launching strikes against Iran.
news.summary: The US and Israel have drawn up plans for a short, intense offensive targeting Iran's nuclear and energy facilities, missiles and drones after the midterms, The New York Times reports; Tehran warns renewed fighting would not be brief
news.author: Daniel Edelson, New York
